value: NG.CASH is a Brazilian digital account built for teenagers and young adults, the people who start their financial life with no bank history. The free account gives a personalised prepaid Mastercard, Pix (including by WhatsApp message), an interest-earning savings pot (Cofrinho), an allowance feature, an app that changes its look with user-chosen skins, and a paid subscription tier priced around R$10 a month. Over time it added consortium financing, insurance, fixed-income investing, an AI assistant and, in 2026, Pix Crédito and a payroll-backed private loan (Crédito CLT). The company earns from payments, the subscription and, increasingly, credit. The story starts with the founders' own YouTube Minecraft channel (Neagle), which two of them created at 15 in 2014: as minors they could not receive their international earnings themselves, a pain they later turned into the Neagle Bank experiment, which opened 70,000 accounts in a day and showed retention among minors at more than twice the market average. The founders, who had also built and sold the banking-as-a-service startup Trampolin to Stone, relaunched it as NG.CASH in August 2021 and reached about 900,000 users in a year, almost all through organic reach and influencer culture rather than paid ads. The Central Bank had published that under 10% of Gen Z had made a Pix, which the founders read as an ignored generation. Traction: more than 2 million users in February 2024, 6 million after absorbing rival Z1's customers in February 2025, more than 7 million in July 2025 and more than 8 million accounts in November 2025, with more than US$2 billion moved. It became a Central Bank-authorised payment institution in 2025 and bought a direct-credit licence from BizCapital. It is backed by a16z, Monashees, NEA, Quantum Light, Endeavor Catalyst, 17Sigma, Daphni and, since September 2026, Blockchain Capital. Next: credit for young adults (the CEO's group targets R$1 billion originated by end of 2027), stablecoin products under a VASP licence, and retaining users as they become adults. Brazil stays the priority; regional expansion is mentioned.

value: The problem: Brazil's Gen Z was a large group the banks ignored. Minors and 18-to-24-year-olds have no credit history, little income, and until recently few ways to hold money or send a Pix; the founders say the Central Bank found fewer than 10% of Gen Z had made a Pix. Parents or big banks served them badly, and big banks treated them as a rounding error. The logic: the founders came from the audience (a YouTube channel with millions of followers, then Trampolin, a banking-as-a-service startup), so they could acquire users organically, speak the user's language and test product ideas cheaply. Their Neagle Bank experiment showed unusually high retention among minors, and Pix made a fast zero-to-Pix account the core product. Why now: Pix (2020) made instant payments free and universal, the Central Bank has opened licences for payment institutions and credit companies, and a generation raised on mobile games already pays subscriptions. Market: our estimate, not a sourced figure. Brazil has roughly 15 million people aged 20 to 24 (IBGE yearbook table) and a similar number aged 15 to 19, so about 30 million, and the company itself speaks of 50 million young people. If a strong outcome means 20 to 30% of that base as active customers (6 to 15 million, against 8 million accounts today) and revenue of R$100 to R$300 a year per active customer from subscription, card, payments and credit, the revenue pool is about R$0.6 to R$4.5 billion a year in Brazil alone; credit is the upside, and the 2027 target of R$1 billion originated is a first step. Comparables: Nubank, and in the US the teen banks Greenlight and Step, show that a youth-first account can become a lifetime primary bank if it keeps users as they age. What is different: distribution through culture (influencers, trap and rap events) and a product that feels like a game, plus its own payment institution and credit licences, instead of a child's savings account; a16z, Monashees and NEA backing add credibility. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed founders who know the audience better than any investor, and a stage where a connector can help (Norte joined the 2022 seed alongside a16z, Monashees and unicorn founders, and its network helps with hiring and funds). Risks: users churn when they turn 18 and large banks and Nubank target the same base; credit to young people with thin files carries default risk and needs capital and regulation compliance; and the newest move into stablecoins distracts from the core.

value: CredAluga is a Brazilian fintech that replaces the guarantor (fiador) and the cash deposit in rental contracts. It works only through real estate agencies, with no intermediaries: the agency offers the product, CredAluga analyses the tenant's risk with its own credit model, and, if the tenant is approved, charges a monthly fee to act as guarantor. If the tenant stops paying, CredAluga pays the owner and the agency on time and takes over the collection. Contracting is 100% digital, the fee can be split into up to 12 instalments, and coverage can reach 35 to 40 times the rent. The line has three products: CredFiança, the traditional fee-based guarantee, now modular, with monthly rates from 8% for the tenant and a recurring commission for the agency; CredReembolsa, with cashback to the tenant and rates from 6%; and Fundo CredAluga, launched at the end of 2024, in which the tenant puts a deposit that is invested in low-risk fixed income, with no monthly fee. The fund turned out to be an easy way in for agencies that did not use the fiança, and add-ons (painting, debt arrangements) are optional. The company was created in 2022 by Daniel Santos and Guilherme Blumer, who come from the real estate market; it started with money from the founders and their families and began operating in the second quarter of 2023, with a little over 500 agencies by October 2024 and a forecast of R$30 million in revenue for 2024, seven times 2023. By September 2025 it said it had more than 30,000 contracts in three years, 1,300 to 1,500 partner agencies in about 500 cities, 200% revenue growth in twelve months, and R$25 million in the fund, aiming at R$1 billion by 2028. The company's own site now claims more than 2,000 agencies. Backers: Caravela Capital, Honey Island by 4UM, Terracota, FJ Labs and Norte in the 2024 seed (R$22 million), Provence Partners, Caravela, Honey Island and Norte in the R$60 million 2025 Series A, and OLX Group, which put US$5 million in as a minority partner in October 2025 and opened the ZAP, Viva Real and OLX portals as a channel. Plans: grow 10 times by 2030, automate more than half of operations by 2026, launch two new rental products, and be the agency's hub for financial products.
note: Pages read: Portas 2025-09-29 (Series A, 30k contracts, 1,300 agencies, fund R$25M, 10x by 2030, automation, R$1bn fund by 2028, 15-20k fitting agencies); Bloomberg Línea 2024-10-28 (origin, operating since Q2 2023, 500 agencies, R$30M forecast, seed investors, 40x coverage); Portas 2025-10-29 (OLX US$5M, 1,500 agencies in 500 cities, portals); credaluga.com.br (products, rates, 2,000 agencies, 12x); earlier claims. value: The problem: renting in Brazil still needs a guarantee. The owner wants a fiador, a cash deposit of up to three months or an insurance policy, and most tenants have no guarantor or cannot put down the money. Around 6 million rental contracts are signed a year, and almost 80% still use the old methods, according to InfoMoney (2025-05-07), which slows deals and favours the big digital platforms over independent agencies. The logic: CredAluga turns the guarantee into a financial product priced by risk, sold through the agency (who gets a recurring commission, so it is aligned to push it), and backed by its own credit analysis, anti-fraud technology and a legal structure for collection. The fund product lets it add a second source of funding and a cheaper entry point. Why now: renting is growing (20.9% of households were rented in the 2022 Census, up from 12.3% in 2000), the fiador is disappearing, and the market's biggest portal owner, OLX Group, chose CredAluga after ending its exclusive partnership with Creditas in October 2025, which gives it distribution to 34,000 portal clients. Market: the press quotes a potential of up to R$36 billion a year in guarantee volume (InfoMoney, an estimate repeated from the companies). Our own arithmetic: 6 million new contracts a year, of which about 80% (4.8 million) lack a modern guarantee; at an assumed rent of R$2,000 and a fee of 6 to 8% a month (the site's rates), a guaranteed contract pays R$1,400 to R$1,900 a year; if CredAluga reached 5 to 10% of those contracts (240,000 to 480,000), annual revenue would be about R$0.3 to R$0.9 billion in Brazil alone, and the company's 10x target from the 2025 base would be in that range. Different: it sells only through agencies (a channel conflict-free for them, unlike marketplaces), offers a modular menu of three guarantees, and has the OLX data and portals; competitors are Loft (500,000 contracts under management in fiança), Creditas, insurers' seguro-fiança and the capitalisation bonds that dominate the market. Fit with Norte (our reading): two founders from the real estate trade who bring a clear distribution plan, investors from Norte's circle (Caravela, Honey Island, Provence, FJ Labs) and a stage where connecting funds and OLX-type partners matters; Norte followed in both the seed and the Series A, a pattern consistent with the Manifesto's 'follower and connector'. Risks: default losses are the business, so one bad vintage or a recession could erase the fee income, and the fund product multiplies liability if it grows to R$1 billion; OLX and Creditas could both distribute competing products, and the company depends on agencies' goodwill.
note: Read: InfoMoney 2025-05-07 (6M contracts, ~80% old methods, up to R$36bn potential), Portas 2025-09-29 (20.9% of households rented, 15-20k fitting agencies, R$60M Series A with Norte), Portas 2025-10-29 (OLX, 34k portal clients, Loft 500k contracts), Bloomberg Línea 2024-10-28 (Norte in seed, 70,000 agencies by Cofeci, 17.3% to 20.2% renters per IBGE), credaluga.com.br (rates 6 and 8% monthly). Arithmetic: 6M x 80% = 4.8M; x 5-10% = 240-480k; x R$2,000 x 6-8% x 12 = R$1,440-1,920 a contract a year; product = R$0.35-0.92bn. Rent level R$2,000 and share 5-10% are our assumptions. R$36bn figure is an estimate by the companies as relayed by the press, not an independent source. Confidence medium: market from press, differentiation from read pages.

value: Flieber is a New York-based software company that tells multichannel commerce brands how much inventory to hold, where and when to reorder. Customers are direct-to-consumer brands, wholesalers and the agencies or aggregators that run many brands, selling on Amazon, Shopify, Walmart, TikTok Shop, eBay, Etsy and BigCommerce. A data layer pulls live sales and stock from every channel and warehouse; a planning engine forecasts demand (including for new products, by comparing them with similar ones) and recommends purchase orders, warehouse transfers and promotions; and workflows carry out what the team approves. The newest version is built for AI agents: the same data can be queried from the Flieber app, Slack, Google Sheets, an API, a CLI or an MCP server, so that Claude, ChatGPT or a company's own agents can answer questions such as whether a promotion will cause a stockout. It sells self-serve plans (the Shopify app listing shows a monthly subscription of roughly US$300 to start, with a free trial) and managed services in which Flieber's planners join the customer's team. The idea came from CEO Fabricio Miranda, a Brazilian who had founded and sold a water-treatment company, worked at a hedge fund, then became a top Amazon seller; he found that sellers spend about 80% of their time on operations rather than selling, and built Flieber in 2019 with CTO Jair Vercosa. By September 2021 clients sold in 15 countries, 400,000 products ran on the platform, 20 million sales orders had been processed, and the system made over 500,000 calculations a day; the company says it has served more than 1,000 brands since 2019. It raised US$12 million in a Series A co-led by GGV Capital and Monashees in 2021 (about US$20 million in total at that time), with Monashees joining the board, to hire data scientists and engineers, improve its data and expand its APIs. Next, per its current site: AI-agent workflows and managed planning on top of the data layer.
note: Pages read: TechCrunch 2021-09-22 (origin, Series A, traction figures, 80% on operations, board); flieber.com homepage 2026 (channels, agents, MCP, managed services, 1,000 brands); Shopify App Store listing (R$1,758.96 a month from, free trial; at roughly 5.9 BRL a dollar about US$300, our conversion; the USD figure comes from a search summary of the same listing). Flieber's own site is undated, so the AI-agent positioning is as of the 2026-11-19 read. Paraphrased.

value: The problem: online selling has become easy, but everything behind it (how much to make or buy, when to order, where to store it, whether a promotion will empty the shelf) is still run in spreadsheets. A brand selling on several channels is always stuck between stockouts, which lose the best-selling product, and overstock, which ties up cash. Miranda says sellers spend about 80% of their time on operations. The logic: pulling live data from every channel and warehouse into one planning engine, then recommending the next best action, turns inventory into a decision made with cash, margin and stockout days in view. Why now: marketplaces and TikTok Shop have multiplied channels, brands are exposed to tariffs, cash cost and long lead times, and AI agents make it possible to ask the plan a question in plain language, which is what the 2026 product is built around. Market: no independent published figure was found, so this is our bottom-up estimate. The product costs about US$300 a month at the entry tier and more for managed services; if the reachable base is 20,000 to 60,000 multichannel brands and agencies worldwide that outgrow spreadsheets (our assumption, not a sourced count) and each pays an average of US$3,000 to US$8,000 a year, the revenue pool is about US$60 million to US$480 million a year; the company says it has served 1,000 brands since 2019, so it holds well under 5% of the low end. A strong outcome would be a leading mid-market planner for e-commerce brands with US$50 to US$100 million of revenue, which is consistent with the pool. What is different: it plans across marketplaces, direct sites and wholesale in one view, includes cash and promotions in the recommendation, and offers planners as a managed service; competitors include Inventory Planner, Cin7, Netstock and the ERP suites, which are not named in the sources read, so this is our reading. Fit with Norte (our reading): a Brazilian-born founder with prior operating experience building from New York, a global market from day one, and investors that Norte's network overlaps with (Monashees co-led the Series A); but the Manifesto says Norte invests early and is a follower, and no source places Norte in Flieber's 2021 round, so the fit is by profile rather than by a documented investment. Risks: a crowded category in which ERPs and Amazon's own tools bundle forecasting; a small base of publicly known customers and no disclosed revenue since 2021; reliance on third-party channel data and APIs; and the pivot toward AI agents is not yet proven.
note: Market is our arithmetic: 20,000 to 60,000 accounts x US$3,000 to 8,000 a year = US$60M to US$480M. The account count and the average price are assumptions; the US$300 monthly entry price is from the Shopify listing (R$1,758.96 read). Competitors named from general knowledge, not read here. No disclosed revenue or customer count since 2021. Pages: TechCrunch 2021-09-22, flieber.com, Shopify App Store. Norte's role: the Series A row has norte_participated UNKNOWN. Confidence low because market size and competitor evidence are not sourced.

value: Carbonext is a Brazilian climate company that develops and sells nature-based carbon credits and, since 2025, a wider set of decarbonisation services. Its core is forest conservation (REDD+) in the Amazon: it pays landowners the opportunity cost of not clearing forest they could legally convert to cattle or soy, monitors the area so it stays standing, and sells the resulting Verra-certified credits (one credit equals one tonne of CO2 not emitted) in the voluntary market. It earns fees for designing and managing the projects and from selling the credits. Large clients such as iFood, Cielo and Raízen get tailored contracts, one-off or multi-year; from 2021 individuals and small businesses can neutralise their footprint with a subscription of about R$60 a month. Its areas were about 1 million hectares in the Amazon in 2021, out of 140 to 150 million hectares the company estimates could be protected through direct payments. The company was founded in 2010 by forest engineer Janaína Dallan, a UN expert on carbon projects and president of the Brazilian Alliance for Nature-Based Solutions, with experience at European carbon firms; her brother Luciano Fonseca, a former Pátria Investimentos private-equity executive, structured the operation in its first 12 months and became co-CEO, and he led the first outside rounds. Funding: a seed from angels in 2021, a R$30 million Series A in September 2021 from more than 20 investors including Canary, Alexia Ventures and FitPart, and R$200 million from Shell in 2022. It was one of 10 startups in the first sustainability edition of the Google for Startups Accelerator in 2022. It has four lines: forest conservation, regenerative agriculture (through a stake in NaturAll Carbon, an Anglo-Brazilian carbon-removal company), a reforestation arm still at an early stage, and NetZero Solutions, which began when it bought 40% of Mangue Tech (an AI carbon-inventory software company founded in 2021 by former Linx executives) in August 2025 with money from the Shell round, keeping the acquired companies independent. It sees Brazil's Law 15,042 on a regulated carbon market as a source of demand, especially from small and medium companies that will need to measure, reduce and offset emissions.
note: Pages read: Brazil Journal 2021-09-01 (model, R$60 subscription, 1M hectares, 140-150M hectare potential, Series A investors, clients, competitors Biofílica and Sustainable Carbon); Brazil Journal 2025-08-05 (Mangue Tech 40%, NaturAll, four segments, Shell money, Law 15.042); carbonext.com.br/en/about (mission, founders' bios, offices). Google for Startups from the existing milestone. Prices are 2021 figures. Paraphrased.

value: The problem: companies that promised to be carbon neutral, and soon those obliged to report under Brazil's regulated-market law, need credible ways to measure, cut and offset emissions, while the world's largest standing forest is under pressure from clearing that landowners can legally do on 20% of their land. The logic: a credit is a payment for the cost of not clearing, so the business works when a trusted party can verify the forest stays and sell the credit at a price above the opportunity cost. Carbonext has done this since 2010 with Verra certification and a founder who sits on UN and Brazilian government advisory bodies, which matters in a market where buyer trust is the scarce asset. Why now: the 2020-21 net-zero pledges lifted demand; Brazil created a regulated carbon market in Law 15.042; and the company is adding measurement software and agriculture-based removals so that it can sell a full package, not just credits. Market: the company estimates that 140 to 150 million hectares of Amazon forest with proven title and clearing risk could be protected through direct payments, and it held about 1 million (under 1%). Our bottom-up illustration, with every input an assumption (we found no read price or yield source): if a strong outcome is 5 to 10 million hectares, with 0.3 to 1.0 tonnes of avoided CO2 sold per hectare a year at US$5 to US$12 a tonne, gross credit sales are about US$7 million to US$120 million a year before the landowner's share, and the other three lines add more, so the pool is mid-size rather than huge. Different: a Brazil-based developer with 15 years of project history, a founder-led credibility, a Shell investor and a plan to own the measure-reduce-offset chain; competitors named in the press are Biofílica (bought by Ambipar) and Sustainable Carbon. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders with deep subject expertise and a finance operator, a network need (international buyers, funds) that a connector can help with, but no source says Norte invested, and the portfolio page lists the company without describing any round; the Manifesto's 'right people at the right time' would fit as a buyer and investor introduction. Risks: voluntary-credit prices and integrity crises (REDD+ credits have been criticised for over-crediting), dependence on a few large buyers, execution across four lines, and the regulated market's rules not yet being clear.
note: 140-150M hectares and the 1M hectares are the company's figures in Brazil Journal 2021-09-01 and 'market will grow 15x by 2030' was Janaína Dallan's claim there. The US$ range is our arithmetic: 5-10M ha x 0.3-1.0 t x US$5-12 = US$7.5M-120M; hectares, yield and price are assumptions, not read. The REDD+ criticism is general knowledge, not a read source. No source names Norte for this company. Confidence low: market and differentiation are mostly the company's own claims.

value: Tractian is an industrial AI company that protects the machines inside factories from unplanned stops. It puts its own wireless sensors on critical equipment such as compressors, chillers, pumps and palletisers; they collect vibration, ultrasound, temperature, current and voltage, and its AI, trained on a large set of industrial failure data, names the likely root cause and recommends an action. The sensors are lent to customers (comodato) and Tractian earns recurring software revenue. It began with mechanical monitoring, which the CEO calls the 'predictive band-aid', and has expanded into what it calls physical AI, covering mechanical, electrical and operational condition plus computer vision; it also sells maintenance-management software and a product that reads manufacturers' manuals to predict faults, launched in the US with partners such as Siemens and Johnson Controls. The idea came from the three founders: Igor Marinelli, who grew up around his father's maintenance work in a paper mill and was building software at 13, Gabriel Lameirinhas, his classmate at the University of São Paulo, and Leonardo Vieira, a salesman whose brother worked in industrial maintenance and who gave them their first client lead. Founded in 2019, they spent the first year on software only, then talked to more than 80 industrial companies and moved to building their own sensors in 2020. Y Combinator took them in the Winter 2021 batch with about 30 industrial customers. Growth since: an office in Mexico in January 2022, the CEO's move to Atlanta in 2024 as the US became the main market, revenue of about US$40 million in 2024 (up 100%), a first acquisition (a roughly 10-person Atlanta startup, for about US$3 million mostly in shares) to reach equipment makers, and, by October 2026, annualised recurring revenue of almost US$100 million (2.5 times in two years), more than 2,000 factories, more than 700 employees, near-breakeven profitability and clients such as Eli Lilly, McKesson, Whirlpool, Coca-Cola bottlers, Cummins and Embraer, plus three large AI data-centre operators. Mid and large companies are about 80% of revenue. It raised a US$130 million Series D at a US$1.4 billion valuation in October 2026, which made it Latin America's most valuable AI company, and plans to let its models act on machines (not just recommend) next year, monitor robots, expand into data centres and reach about US$500 million of ARR and a US listing in three to five years.
note: Pages read: Brazil Journal 2026-11-04 (ARR, 2,000 factories, physical AI, comodato, plans, USP origin); Tractian blog on the Series D, 2026-10-22 (customers, 700 employees, offices, founder's father); Norte case post 'Tractian: Brio' (founders' origins, Leo's first lead); Bloomberg Línea 2025-04-25 (US$40M 2024 revenue, acquihire, manuals product, 80% of revenue mid/large, move to Atlanta); existing claims for YC, Mexico office, 2020 sensor pivot. Paraphrased.

value: The problem: factories run on machines that wear out and fail, and most maintenance hours still go on reactive fixes. Siemens' True Cost of Downtime (January 2026, as cited in Tractian's Series D post) puts unplanned downtime at about 11% of annual revenue for the world's 500 largest industrial companies, around US$1.4 trillion a year; industrial assets average 24 years of use, and Deloitte projects more than 2.1 million manufacturing jobs may go unfilled by 2030, so the know-how of retiring technicians leaves the plant. The logic: cheap sensors plus a model trained on failures can tell a technician what is wrong and what to do, so the software scales where experts do not; lending the sensors removes the customer's upfront cost and creates subscription revenue, and each installed machine adds data that makes the next diagnosis better. Why now: connected sensors and wireless networks are cheap, AI models can read manuals and sensor data together, and AI data centres and reshoring are driving a build-out of critical physical infrastructure where downtime is not acceptable. Market: the downtime figure shows the size of the problem, not of the software market. Our bottom-up estimate: about 2,000 customers and nearly US$100 million of ARR imply roughly US$50,000 a customer. If 100,000 to 200,000 mid-size and large industrial sites worldwide (our assumption) could pay US$30,000 to US$100,000 a year, the reachable pool is about US$3 billion to US$20 billion; the company's own target of US$500 million of ARR is roughly 2.5 to 17% of that. Different: its own hardware (rather than integrating other vendors' sensors), the multimodal data set, a field sales model with US regional hubs that raised conversion by 45%, and the partnerships with machine makers who might otherwise be rivals. Comparables abroad: Samsara (IoT operations, listed in the US) and Augury (US machine-health company, also raised hundreds of millions), both named from general knowledge, not read here. Fit with Norte (our reading): Norte's own case post describes the three founders' energy ('brio') and shared industrial background, and the Manifesto's focus on obsessed founders who know more than the investor; Norte took part early (2021 pre-seed and seed) and again in the Series D, which fits its follower and connector role with Y Combinator and later funds. Risks: hardware and field-service costs weigh on margins (the company says it is near breakeven, not yet profitable); well-funded rivals and the machine makers themselves can build the same monitoring; revenue is increasingly concentrated in US industrial and AI-infrastructure cycles; and the move to let AI act on machines raises safety and liability stakes.
note: Siemens US$1.4T / 11% figure and Deloitte 2.1M jobs figure are read only as quoted in Tractian's own blog post (the Siemens and Deloitte reports were not opened), so they are company-relayed. Bottom-up: US$100M / 2,000 = US$50k; 100-200k sites x US$30-100k = US$3-20bn; site count and price are our assumptions; 500M/3B = 17% and 500M/20B = 2.5%, i.e. 2.5% to 17%. 45% conversion gain, 80% mid/large share and acquihire from Bloomberg Línea 2025-04-25. Confidence medium: market size relayed and assumed, differentiation from read pages.

value: Jota is a Brazilian fintech that gives micro-entrepreneurs and small businesses a digital account run through an AI assistant, in WhatsApp or in its own conversational app (launched in February 2026). The owner opens an account in a few minutes by starting a chat, then pays suppliers by text, voice note or a photo of a bill, charges customers with a Pix QR code, boleto or card (up to 12 instalments), records who owes money, and asks the assistant for revenue reports, calculations and tips; the name plays on 'PJ' (pessoa jurídica). Extra agents handle calendar reminders, scheduled payments and receipts, and overdraft alerts through Open Finance. Most features are free; the main income today comes from FalaTap, a function that turns a phone into a card machine, launched in 2026 (Brazil Journal says about a month before June 2026, Startups.com.br says the first quarter), plus receivables advance; credit tied to the overdraft alert is planned, and a 'reverse trial' subscription (full product free up to a daily limit, then paid) comes with Jota 3.0. The assistant runs on Meta's WhatsApp APIs and OpenAI models, with Jota training its own finance model on top. Founder Davi Holanda, from Ceará, spent six years at PagBank leading more than 15 products (including its card-machine and prepaid and credit card lines), left right after its 2018 IPO, and helped found Bankly, a banking-as-a-service company bought by Méliuz and later sold to Banco BV; he created Jota in July 2024 with Marcelo Leite. It launched publicly on 24 January 2025 after a beta with friends and family, with a US$8.9 million seed led by Maya Capital (HOF Capital, BigBets, Alter Global, Bogari, Norte Ventures and angels), which the press also puts at R$60 million. By June 2026 it had about 300,000 clients, mostly small businesses and freelancers, and R$3.5 billion of annualised payment volume; it aimed at R$50 million of annualised revenue by December, 1 million clients and more than R$10 billion of volume in 2026. In June 2026 it raised a US$30 million (R$150 million) Series A led by Haun Ventures, its first Brazilian investment, at a US$185 million post-money valuation, with HOF, Alter Global and Greyhound Capital. The money goes to Jota 2.0, a proactive agent that sorts expenses and acts without being asked (about five times more engagement in early tests), to credit, and to hires: in November 2026 it named a CTO, CFO and its first head of HR.
note: Pages read: Brazil Journal 2026-06-29 (products, FalaTap, founder history, 300k clients, Jota 3.0, Haun round); Brazil Journal 2025-01-24 (launch, seed investors incl. Norte, OpenAI/Meta stack); Startups.com.br 2026-06-29 (app in February, Q1 FalaTap, R$3.5bn TPV, 2026 targets, R$60M seed); Finsiders 2026-11-13 (executive hires, July 2024 creation); earlier claims. Paraphrased. Client and volume figures are the company's. FalaTap timing conflicts between the two June 2026 articles.

value: The problem: Brazil's micro-entrepreneurs run their business from the phone and a notebook. They charge by Pix over WhatsApp, track debts on paper, and use banks whose apps were built for individuals, while big banks treat them as a low-priority segment. The Maya Capital partner called the segment very under-served and not a priority for large banks. The logic: if the interface is the chat the customer already uses all day, onboarding takes minutes, the assistant does tasks (pay, charge, record, remind) instead of showing menus, and the account becomes the source of data for credit and acquiring offers; the founder's thesis is that after branches, internet banking and apps, the next interface is an AI agent that works continuously for the client. Why now: Pix made instant payments free and universal, WhatsApp's business APIs and language models make a reliable conversational agent possible and cheap to build, and Open Finance opens the data for overdraft and credit. Market: the Receita Federal's government panel (as reported by Brasil 61 in June 2025) shows 23.5 million active companies in Brazil and 12.7 million of them MEIs, half of all firms; many more are micro and small businesses and freelancers. Our estimate of the revenue pool: if a strong outcome is 2 to 3 million active clients (about 15 to 25% of MEIs, our assumption, against about 300,000 today) each yielding R$200 to R$600 a year from acquiring, receivables advance, credit and subscription (our assumption; the company's own R$50M target on 300,000 to 1 million clients implies about R$50 to R$170 a client in 2026), the pool is about R$0.4 to R$1.8 billion a year, with credit as the upside. What is different: a conversational-first account with a product leader from PagBank's growth era, a free entry that spreads quickly (about 300,000 clients in 17 months), and tier-one backers new to Brazil (Haun, HOF). Competitors: PagBank, Stone, Mercado Pago, Nubank PJ and CloudWalk's InfinitePay, named as card-machine rivals in the press, are far larger and chase the same segment. Fit with Norte (our reading): a repeat founder with an operating record and a clear view that the interface is changing, an early stage where Norte joined the seed beside Maya, and a network need around funds and hiring that suits its connector role. Risks: the free product has to be monetised, and most revenue so far comes from a card-machine product that competes with giants on price; dependence on WhatsApp and one AI vendor; credit to micro-businesses has losses; and a young company (2 years old) is growing fast with new executives.
note: Read: Brasil 61 2025-06-15 (23,452,457 active companies, 12,713,060 MEIs, per the Painel de Dados do Governo Federal); Brazil Journal 2025-01-24 (Maya quote, stack, Norte in seed); Brazil Journal and Startups.com.br 2026-06-29 (clients, TPV, targets, Series A). Arithmetic: 2-3M clients = 16-24% of 12.7M MEIs; x R$200-600 = R$0.4-1.8bn. Share and per-client yield are assumptions; the company's R$50M ARR target divided by 300k-1M clients gives R$50-170. Competitors named from the Startups.com.br article (PagSeguro and CloudWalk) and general knowledge (the rest), not otherwise read. Confidence medium: market from a read government panel, the rest assumed.

value: Stay is a Brazilian fintech that lets employers offer corporate private pension plans (previdência) as a benefit, in the way Vestwell and Human Interest do in the United States. It works as the connecting layer between companies of any size and the leading insurers: the employer picks a plan, the employee enrols and manages the plan, balance, contributions, withdrawals and life-insurance cover through WhatsApp, and the HR team gets data about its people. Products today: private pension plans, group life insurance, a financial-health programme (check-up, data for HR and compliance with the NR-1 workplace-risk rule), and long-term incentive plans (ILP) and executive pay design, used to retain talent; the site says a pension strategy can save the company about 40% against paying the same amount in salary, through tax efficiency. It earns fees on the plans and services sold to companies, and the plans are issued through an insurer partnership with Zurich Seguros that began in 2024. It was started in 2023 by a team of tech and finance executives: CEO Tsai Chi-Yu (formerly Morgan Stanley, Uber and the defunct Hash), Nicolas Frajhof (operations), Pedro Iglesias (business development) and Caio Elias, who appears as a founder in 2024 coverage and as CTO in 2026. The pitch rests on a gap: fewer than 3% of Brazilian workers have corporate pension, against 70% to 90% in comparable economies, and the CEO ties the product to record household indebtedness. In October 2024, a little over a year in, it had about 10 people, dozens of clients (a law firm, an operator and a hospital-products multinational) and raised a R$15 million seed led by MAYA Capital and Better Tomorrow Ventures, with 17Sigma, Grão, Ralicap, Sequoia's scout fund and the founders of Vestwell and Human Interest; it planned to double the team and grow clients tenfold. In September 2026 it raised R$30 million in a round led by Citrino (a multi-family office linked to leading business families), with Norte, 17Sigma and BTV, and reported assets under management up 31 times since its start (the site says R$48 million for 127 companies and 12,400 employees), clients such as iFood, Claro, Milky Moo and the Araújo Jorge cancer hospital, and a goal of more than 100 corporate clients by the end of 2026. It will use the money to move beyond traditional pensions into financial-health tools and ILP.
note: Pages read: Times Brasil 2026-09-25 (round, <3% penetration, Zurich 2024, 31x AUM, client names, 100 clients target); Startups.com.br 2024-10-30 (origins, founders' backgrounds, seed, 2024 client names, Vestwell and Human Interest, 10 staff); stay.com.br homepage (products, WhatsApp, NR-1, 40% saving claim, R$48M / 127 companies from the existing claim); earlier claims. Caio Elias status is unclear between the two articles. Paraphrased. Figures are the company's own.

value: The problem: almost no Brazilian worker saves for retirement through the employer. The CEO says fewer than 3% of workers have corporate pension, against 70% to 90% in comparable economies, while household debt is at record levels; employers compete for talent with salary alone and lose people. The logic: private pension is tax-advantaged for the employer and the employee, so paying part of the package that way can cost the company less than the same amount in salary (Stay claims about 40% saving), and it also works as a retention tool, especially through long-term incentive plans. The hard parts are the paperwork, the insurer's systems and getting employees to enrol, which Stay solves with a digital platform and a WhatsApp interface on top of insurers' plans; it keeps the trust-heavy part (the plan and the insurer) with established partners such as Zurich, and sells the experience and the advice. Why now: record household debt, a tight market for talent, higher interest rates that make fixed-income savings visible, and WhatsApp as the default service channel. Market: IBGE (via Correio, 2026-10-30) counts 39.4 million private-sector employees with a formal contract, a record. If 25 to 30% of them (about 10 to 12 million, our assumption) work for employers large or mid-sized enough to offer a plan, contribute an average R$300 to R$500 a month (our assumption), and Stay captures a distribution and platform fee of 0.5% to 1% of assets a year, then a fully penetrated plan base would carry about R$36 to R$72 billion of new contributions a year and, after several years of accumulation, hundreds of billions in assets; at a 10% share of that pool, Stay's fee revenue would be of the order of R$0.2 to R$1 billion a year. Today it has about R$48 million of assets for 127 companies (about R$3,900 an employee, per the company), so the opportunity is mostly ahead. What is different: it is employer-first and digital, packages pension with life insurance, financial health and ILP, runs on WhatsApp, and is backed by operators of the same model in the US (Vestwell and Human Interest founders are investors) and by Citrino's family-office network, which matters in a trust business. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders with a finance and tech record who found a clear structural gap, and a stage where a connector can bring funds and business families to the cap table, as the Citrino-led round shows; Norte took part in the 2026 round. Risks: revenue is tied to assets and takes years to build; Stay depends on insurers such as Zurich for the product and its economics; sales cycles with HR and finance are long; and incumbents such as banks' own pension arms and benefit platforms could sell the same package.
note: Read: Times Brasil 2026-09-25 (<3% vs 70-90%, Norte in round, AUM multiple); Startups.com.br 2024-10-30 (<10% have any private pension per the CEO, 90% over 25 do not plan per Maya, Vestwell and Human Interest founders); Correio 24 Horas 2026-10-30 (IBGE: 39.4M formal private employees); stay.com.br (40% saving claim, R$48M / 127 companies from earlier claim). Arithmetic: 39.4M x 25-30% = 9.9-11.8M; x R$300-500 x 12 = R$36-71bn a year; fee 0.5-1% of assets; 10% share. Share of eligible workers, contribution and fee level are our assumptions, not read. Confidence low: market is assumption-driven and differentiation rests on company statements.

value: tapi is a payments-infrastructure company that lets banks, fintechs and large platforms offer bill payments, mobile top-ups, digital gift cards and cash-in and cash-out through a single API, across Argentina, Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru. Behind that one connection it holds the links to thousands of service companies (utilities, telecoms), physical networks (OXXO, Walmart, 7-Eleven and Tiendas 3B in Mexico) and banks, so a customer such as Nubank, Mercado Pago, Santander, Banamex or HSBC does not have to integrate each one. It also sells tapipay, a collections platform for small and mid-size companies, financiers and insurers that charge on a recurring basis, which automates billing and connects to the banking system and every payment method. It earns from the volume it routes (our reading; the sources do not state its fees). The company began in August 2019 when Tomás Mindlin, a returning Londoner inspired by Revolut, and his childhood friend Kevin Litvin, then in Madrid, met in Buenos Aires to build a consumer wallet called Tap; Nicolás Andriano, a classmate of Mindlin from ITBA, joined months later to lead technology and product. The wallet reached 700,000 users in about a year and a half, but the team found that the payment providers' systems were built for shops with a few hundred transactions a day, not for fintechs, and they had to rebuild their suppliers' technology. They pivoted from consumers to B2B and spent their first operating year building coverage in five countries before signing a first client, on the bet that the large fintechs (Mercado Libre, Nubank, Ualá) needed regional payment rails. A US$9 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz in 2022 and a US$22 million Series A led by Kaszek in mid-2024 followed; in July 2025 it bought two business units of Arcus, a Mastercard company, in Mexico (bill payments, top-ups, gift cards and cash services), its first acquisition; and in February 2026 it raised a US$27 million Series B led by Kaszek with Endeavor Catalyst and Latitud, bringing the total above US$60 million. Mexico is now its main market, where it says 85% of payments are still in cash and the market is three times Argentina's. It reports more than 250 million transactions and over US$6 billion of volume a year, 20,000 service companies and 70,000 physical points, ten times growth in billing and volume in under 18 months, and profitability. More than 70% of staff are in technology. The funds go to new products, scaling tapipay and the Mexican network.
note: Pages read: Forbes Argentina 2025-08-14 (origin, wallet, pivot, five countries, Arcus, Mexico 85% cash); LatamFintech 2026-02-04 (Series B, volumes, clients, networks, tapipay, 10x growth, profitability, 70% tech staff); earlier claims. Paraphrased. The fee model is our inference. Figures are the company's.

value: The problem: Latin American payment systems are fragmented. Each country has its own utilities, bill-payment rails, cash networks and top-up providers, and a bank or fintech that wants to let customers pay a bill or deposit cash in a shop has to integrate dozens of them, each with old technology that was not built for digital scale. In Mexico, the founders say, 85% of payments are still in cash. The logic: be the single connection. Once tapi has built the network (it began in five countries before it had a client), every new client's volume uses the same rails, so the cost per transaction falls and the network becomes hard to copy; owning the infrastructure (and buying Arcus' Mexican units) lets it keep the margin instead of reselling someone else's. Why now: fintechs and neobanks are scaling across the region and need cash and bill-payment features to serve the unbanked, and Mastercard sold off regional units, leaving room for a local specialist. Market: no independent market-size figure was read. Our estimate is from the company's volume: more than US$6 billion across 250 million transactions is about US$24 per transaction; with a revenue take of 0.3% to 0.8% of volume (our assumption) that is roughly US$18 million to US$48 million a year now. The company grew ten times in under 18 months; if volume reaches US$30 to US$60 billion a year (5 to 10 times today, our scenario, which would still be a small slice of Mexico's cash payments) the revenue pool would be about US$90 million to US$480 million a year. What is different: an own, regional network built before demand, direct links to the physical networks and utilities, and a collections product for businesses; the competitors are local aggregators and bill-payment providers (such as Arcus before the sale, Pagos Inteligentes and others), named from general knowledge, not from the sources read. Reported profitability is unusual for a venture-backed payments company and shows discipline. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who pivoted early on what customers taught them, a stage and region where a connector can bring Latin American funds and clients (Kaszek, Endeavor Catalyst and Latitud are in the network), and an infrastructure business that grows with the fintechs Norte also backs. No source says Norte invested in tapi, so we do not claim a role. Risks: thin margins and customer concentration (a few large fintechs and banks), integration and regulatory complexity in five countries, the Mexican strategy depends on integrating the Arcus units, and the cash-to-digital shift (Pix-like instant payment systems, such as Mexico's CoDi and SPEI) could shrink the cash and bill-payment volume over time.
note: Arithmetic: US$6bn / 250M = US$24; 0.3-0.8% x US$6bn = US$18-48M; US$30-60bn x 0.3-0.8% = US$90-480M. The take rate and the volume scenario are assumptions, not read. 85% cash and three-times-Argentina are Litvin's statements in Forbes Argentina 2025-08-14. Competitors, CoDi and SPEI are general knowledge, not read. Norte: the three Rounds are UNKNOWN in rounds.csv. Pages: Forbes Argentina, LatamFintech. Confidence low.

value: idwall was a Brazilian regtech that helped companies know who they were dealing with and stop identity fraud. Its platform covered document validation, facial biometrics, background and compliance checks on people and companies (it says it had processed data on nearly all Brazilians and on 18 million companies), and configurable digital-onboarding flows; it also had a consumer identity app, MeuID, which an investor from GGV described in 2021 as potentially the first true super-app in Latin America. It sold mainly to businesses and earned from usage-based and subscription fees (our reading; the sources do not state its pricing). Lincoln Ando (CEO) and Raphael Melo founded it in São Paulo in mid-2016. It backed early momentum with a 500 Startups investment, a Series A led by Monashees and Canary in 2018, a US$10 million Series B led by Qualcomm Ventures in 2019 (with ONEVC, GGV, Globo's Ithaca and others), and a R$210 million Series C in June 2021 led by Endurance with GGV, Península, Monashees, Canary, Qualcomm, ONEVC, Ithaca and Norte; the 2021 round came when it had more than 300 customers including 15 banks (two of the three largest) and seven financial unicorns such as Cielo, Ebanx, iFood, Loggi and Quinto Andar, and a strategic partnership with Mastercard. By 2026 it had more than 400 customers, among them Bradesco Saúde, SulAmérica, Shopee, QuintoAndar, Globoplay and Claro, had raised about R$260 million in its first ten years, and said it had helped avoid more than R$8 billion in fraud and had received more than 700 million queries. It competed with Unico, a Brazilian unicorn in the same field, and CERTTA (formerly CAF). In May 2026 Serasa Experian, Brazil's largest datatech, agreed to buy it, to strengthen its authentication and anti-fraud range after buying ClearSale in 2024 for R$2 billion; terms were not disclosed, press sources put the price at R$400 million (Valor's Pipeline) or R$450 million (Startups.com.br), and a venture investor told Bloomberg Línea such a figure suggests some investors may have got back about what they put in. CADE cleared the deal without restrictions and Serasa Experian completed it on 1 July 2026; idwall stays in Serasa's identity, biometrics and onboarding offering.
note: Pages read: Bloomberg Línea 2026-05-08 (acquisition, price reports, cap table, competitors, customers, R$260M raised, ClearSale R$2bn); Serasa Experian press room 2026-07-01 (completion, 700M queries, scope); Finsiders 2021-06-02 (Series C, investors incl. Norte, MeuID, 300 clients, Mastercard); earlier claims (2016 founding, 2018-2019 rounds, 500 Startups). Paraphrased. The pricing model is our inference. Whether 500 Startups was an accelerator or only an investor is unresolved.

value: The problem: digital services (fintechs, marketplaces, delivery apps) need to open accounts and sign up customers in minutes, but Brazil has a large amount of identity fraud, documents are easy to fake, and checking people means querying many public and private databases. Doing it in-house is slow, costly and a compliance risk. The logic: an API that unites document and biometric validation with background checks, plus the data to decide, lets a company onboard a real person quickly and prove it to a regulator; each client's queries improve the models, and the customer base compounds (more than 700 million queries, which the company ties to more than R$8 billion in fraud avoided). Why now: Pix and digital banks created an onboarding rush in 2018-2021, regulators required know-your-customer controls, and AI increased the sophistication of fraud, which Serasa cites as a reason for its purchase in 2026. Market: no independent figure was read. Our estimate is bottom-up: Brazil has several thousand regulated financial institutions and fintechs, large marketplaces and insurers that onboard at scale; if 3,000 to 10,000 companies (our assumption) each spend R$100,000 to R$1 million a year on identity verification and fraud prevention, the pool is about R$0.3 to R$10 billion a year. The market evidence we did read is an outcome: Serasa bought idwall for a reported R$400 to R$450 million after ClearSale for R$2 billion, showing a strategic buyer values the category, and that idwall's own result was modest. What was different: a wide offering (document, biometrics, background and onboarding in one), a strong list of financial clients, and well-known backers (Qualcomm, GGV, Endurance, Monashees, Canary); competitors Unico (unicorn) and CERTTA/CAF were larger or better funded in some segments. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who built a regulated, data-heavy product in a segment that fintechs needed, and a follow-on role in the large 2021 round alongside Endurance and GGV, where Norte's network connects funds to the cap table; this is consistent with the Manifesto's 'follower and connector' stance, not Norte's statement. Risks that materialised or remain: strong competition (Unico, CAF) and price pressure on a commoditising check; clients who can build in-house; and, as a venture outcome, a sale at about R$400 to R$450 million against R$260 million raised, which is below what the 2021 round implied, so late investors may not have earned a multiple.
note: Read: Bloomberg Línea 2026-05-08 (price reports, competitors, R$260M raised, investor comment on value), Finsiders 2021-06-02 (clients, Norte in Series C, MeuID), Serasa Experian 2026-07-01 (700M queries, fraud context). Market arithmetic: 3,000-10,000 firms x R$100k-1M = R$0.3-10bn; firm count and spend are our assumptions, not read. The claim that the sale price is below the 2021 round's implied value is our inference from the Bloomberg Línea investor comment, as no valuation for 2021 was read. Confidence low.

value: Kolors is a Mexican mobility company that runs bus transport without owning a single bus. It partners with small, medium and large operators who own and drive the vehicles, while Kolors does the rest through its technology: route and schedule planning, pricing, tracking, customer service, marketing and sales. The CEO compares the model to Uber's. It started with intercity passenger routes in Mexico, which it called a 'smart-bus platform' or an airline on wheels: virtual stops in malls and hotels, on-board attendants, Wi-Fi and snack sales, and a rewards programme; it carried more than 7 million passengers in 2023, over 70% of them millennials and Gen Z, and ran a pilot between Los Angeles and Las Vegas. More recently it has moved to employee transport, selling recurring contracts to companies that need to move workers to the same place at the same time every day (industrial parks, production lines, remote plants); by October 2026 it operated in more than 50 Mexican cities, adding new ones every month, and says it can open a city in a week or less. It uses AI for several years in routing, vehicle-size choice and scheduling, and in one example it solved a client's office parking jam by finding pick-up bays about 500 metres from the building. It earned from bookings and onboard sales on the intercity routes and now from corporate contracts (our reading of the sources). The company was founded in 2020 by Rodrigo Martínez, a third-generation bus operator, and Anca Gardea, during the pandemic. It raised a seed (Alumni Ventures and Expa) and, in June 2022, a US$20 million Series A led by UP.Partners with Maniv Mobility, Toyota Ventures, K5 Global and Mazapil, plus existing investors including Tuesday Capital, Expa, Lowercase, Moving Capital, MGV, Brainstorm Ventures, Bling Capital and Amplifica, for US$26 million in total, to expand in Mexico, Latin America and cross-border US travel and to push toward electric fleets. In 2026 the CEO is weighing expansion outside Mexico, starting with industrial peripheries, but no countries or dates are given. We found no verifiable funding or revenue figures after 2022, and the date of the shift from intercity to staff transport is not stated.
note: Pages read: Ecosistema Startup 2026-10-22 (employee transport, 50 cities, AI, expansion plans, week-to-open claim); PR Newswire 2022-06-03 (Series A, model, founders, 2020, millions of passengers, onboard sales, electrification); Descubre.vc 2025-07-10 (7M passengers in 2023, 70% Gen Z and millennials, Los Angeles-Las Vegas pilot, Kolors Rewards); earlier claims. Paraphrased. Company figures. The model's current revenue is our inference.

value: The problem: in Mexico and much of Latin America, intercity and staff bus transport runs on small, individually owned operators with manual planning and uneven service, while factories and offices must bring workers in daily around the clock, and tens of thousands of kilometres of corridors lack a good option. The logic: separate the vehicle from the platform. Operators keep the capital and the driving; Kolors sells planning, data, customer experience and trust, so it can scale without buying fleets, and employee-transport contracts are recurring, predictable and tied to a daily need. Why now: the pandemic-era launch grew fast (millions of passengers in a short time, said Maniv's principal), mobility investors backed the asset-light model, and a nearshoring-driven rise in Mexican industry gives staff transport a bigger base of customers. Market: no independent size was found for Mexican staff transport. The only figure read is a global ride-hailing value of US$4.17 billion in 2026 (Mordor Intelligence, relayed by Ecosistema Startup), which is a different market, and an IDB statement that Latin American transport needs could double by 2050. Our rough estimate: if 1 to 2 million Mexican workers use employer-provided transport (our assumption) at US$40 to US$100 a month per rider (our assumption), the spend is about US$0.5 to US$2.4 billion a year; a platform taking a 10 to 20% margin on a 10% share would earn about US$5 to US$50 million. This is a niche that can be profitable, not a huge one, unless the model moves to more countries. What is different: the asset-light model, the AI routing and the speed of opening cities (a week), plus a founder from a bus-operating family and a history of intercity data; competitors are local staff-transport firms and the operators themselves, not named in the sources. Fit with Norte (our reading): a founder with deep sector roots and an operator's pragmatism, in a region where a connector can help with funds and corporate clients; however, no source places Norte in either round and the Manifesto's stage and size focus is only loosely matched, so this fit is weak. Risks: thin margins and dependence on operators' service quality (the experience is shared between two companies), concentration on a few corporate clients, little public information on profitability or funding since 2022, and the pivot away from the intercity thesis the investors backed.
note: Read: Ecosistema Startup 2026-10-22 (Mordor US$4.17bn ride-hailing and IDB demand doubling, both relayed; risks of shared experience stated there), PR Newswire 2022-06-03, Descubre.vc 2025-07-10. Arithmetic: 1-2M riders x US$40-100 x 12 = US$0.48-2.4bn; 10% share = US$48-240M gross bookings; margin 10-20% = US$5-48M. Rider count, price and margin are our assumptions, not read. Norte: both Rounds UNKNOWN in rounds.csv; no source names Norte. Confidence low.

value: Norma is a São Paulo startup that applies AI to Brazilian tax compliance, which its founders describe as the most complex tax regulation in the world. It says it is neither a law firm nor 'one more software': it was founded by engineers and tax specialists to turn tax rules into decision infrastructure for companies. It has two products. Malha Fiscal reads all of a company's tax documents against Brazilian tax regulation and quantifies, in reais, both opportunities to cut the tax burden and tax risks, leaving the company to decide what to do. Conciliação da Apuração Assistida rebuilds in near real time the company's IBS/CBS assessment (the new consumption taxes from the tax reform) from its tax documents and events and points out differences with the figures of the tax authority, before they become a cost or a fine. The platform also updates product registers in minutes instead of days, validates invoices in one click, reads XML and SPED files, handles unlimited company registrations (CNPJs) and multiple simultaneous users, connects to ERPs such as TOTVS, Oracle and SAP without migration, and offers custom integrations and expert support. It offers a free diagnostic report in seven days. We read no pricing; revenue most likely comes from software and service contracts (our reading). The founders, CEO Renato Sanabria (ex-ITA), CFO André Corrêa (ex-USP) and CTO Bruno Assis (ex-USP), saw repeatedly the same pattern in companies: outdated product registers, constant tax changes, a flood of invoices, and teams spending hours putting out fires. Work started in 2023 and the company was registered in April 2024. Its site says it has invested R$10 million in technology, monitors about 5,000 companies and has identified R$455 million of risk and R$684 million of opportunities (all unaudited company figures). Its LinkedIn page showed about 10 employees in November 2026. Customers named on the site are mid-sized Brazilian distributors and food companies; in November 2026 the company said that, with its AI, one of the main supermarket chains of Espírito Santo recovered about R$500,000 a month in tax credits that would otherwise have been lost from January, and it was featured in the ABRAS retail magazine SuperHiper and in Portal Contábeis' guide on assisted assessment. The CBS starts in January 2027, which is the commercial window it is working toward. No funding round has been found.
note: Pages read: norma.com.br (products, figures, 'founded by engineers and tax specialists', free diagnostic, ERP integrations); LinkedIn company page and 20 latest posts via Linked API, 2026-11-20 (workflowId wf-81a578fe-b655-47f5-bb88-ec181f8d3f24: description, 10 employees, supermarket chain R$500k a month claim, SuperHiper and Portal Contábeis posts, CBS January 2027 calendar); earlier claims for founders and dates. Paraphrased. All figures are the company's. The startups.com.br item 'Norma sai enquanto a OAB-SP disputa ... com a Enter' concerns a different company, a legaltech named Norma, and was not used.

value: The problem: Brazil's tax system is among the most complex in the world, and companies handle it with spreadsheets and legacy systems while the tax authority has built a sophisticated cross-checking system (the 'malha fiscal'). The site claims tax litigation equals about 75% of GDP against 0.3% in the OECD, a figure we could not verify. Product registers go stale, rules change all the time, and teams spend hours fixing errors that become overpaid tax or fines. The logic: an AI that reads every invoice against the rules can find credits the company did not claim and risks it did not see, and can show the value in reais, so the sale is easy to justify (a free diagnostic in seven days, then a share of the value found, as we read the model). Why now: the tax reform replaces several taxes with the IBS and CBS from 2027 (the CBS starts in January 2027 and the government has refused to postpone it, as Norma's own November 2026 post reports), which forces every company to review its registers, rebuild its assessment and compare it with the tax authority's, and creates a large wave of work for 2026 and 2027. Market: no published size was read. Our estimate: if 30,000 to 60,000 Brazilian companies large enough to need automated tax review (our assumption) each pay R$30,000 to R$150,000 a year, the revenue pool is about R$0.9 to R$9 billion a year; Norma says it monitors 5,000 companies today, which would be about 8 to 17% of that count if all paid, though most are likely free diagnostics. What could make it special: tax-specific AI trained for Brazilian rules rather than a general tool, the reconciliation with the authority's figures, and integrations with the ERPs companies already use; competitors are the large tax-software vendors, big accounting firms and tax-tech startups, not named in the sources read. Fit with Norte (our reading): a team of technical founders attacking a deep, regulated problem at a moment of forced change, in an area where a connector can bring clients and hiring; but no source places Norte in Norma, no round was found, and the company has about 10 staff, so this is an early, unproven thesis. Risks: the tax reform could be simplified or delayed, large competitors (including the tax authority's own calculator and ERP vendors) could give away what Norma sells, AI errors in tax advice carry legal liability, and a sale cycle built around one regulatory deadline may leave revenue lumpy after 2027.
note: Read: norma.com.br; Linked API company page and posts, 2026-11-20 (workflowId wf-81a578fe-b655-47f5-bb88-ec181f8d3f24); search results on tax reform (Migalhas, COAD, NetCPA) not opened. 75% of GDP vs 0.3% OECD is the company's own claim and unverified. Arithmetic: 30,000-60,000 x R$30k-150k = R$0.9-9bn; firm count and price are assumptions; 5,000/60,000 = 8%, 5,000/30,000 = 17%. The contract model (diagnostic then share of value) is our reading, not stated. No funding found and no source names Norte. Confidence low.

value: Legiti was a Brazilian antifraud startup for online merchants. It connected to a client's site or app through an API, collected data on how each user behaved, and scored every transaction with a predictive model built on thousands of features (more than 3,000 in 2020 and more than 4,000 by 2022), refined every day: how many purchases in the last 24 hours, how long a user spent on each page, how far the delivery address was from the buyer's IP location. The aim was to block real fraud, which produces chargebacks, without blocking legitimate buyers, the 'false positives' that Brazil Journal said made up about two thirds of the R$9 billion a year that Latin American banks and retailers lost to e-commerce fraud. Clients paid a monthly fee for each transaction analysed; the first were mostly delivery and pet-product companies (Zee.Now, Shipp, then ZeeDog, Americanas Delivery, Petz, Daki and Rei do Pitaco). For Zee.Now, the pet-products e-commerce, it cut chargebacks by 64% and lifted sales conversion by 1.34 percentage points. The founders, Pedro Sanzovo (Brazilian) and Pearson Henri (American), met on their first day at Stanford, both worked for about three years at Palantir, and set up Legiti in São Paulo in June 2019, first thinking of working as freelancers until they saw how many scams hit Brazilian platforms, which usually paid the bill themselves. It raised a US$2.5 million seed in 2020 led by Kaszek Ventures with Global Founders Capital, Iporanga Ventures and Norte Ventures, and a R$42 million round in January 2022 led by Kaszek with GFC, Iporanga and Picus Capital. In January 2022 it had 13 customers, had prevented more than R$53 million of fraud, had 40 staff and planned 65, at least 50 customers and R$3 million of annual revenue for 2022. In March 2023 the US fraud-protection company Signifyd announced it was adding Legiti's engineers, data scientists and customer-success experts, including both founders, to its team and opening a São Paulo R&D hub; the announcement is a team hire, not a stated acquisition of the company, and we found no later activity or product from Legiti itself.

Paraphrased. Company figures.

value: The problem: in Brazil, e-commerce platforms usually absorb the cost of card fraud and of the filters meant to stop it. Brazil Journal (2020) reported that fraud attempts happen every 16 seconds in Latin American e-commerce and cost banks and retailers about R$9 billion a year, of which an estimated two thirds is false positives (good customers blocked) and only one third is real chargebacks, so classic rules-based filters lose money in both directions. The logic: a model that learns each user's normal behaviour from many signals, and adapts daily as fraudsters change tactics ('an infinite game of chess', as the founder said), can approve more good orders and block more bad ones; the first clients (delivery apps with high fraud and thin margins) would feel the gain in conversion and chargebacks at once. Why now: the pandemic moved sales online (Canaltech), Brazilian instant payment and card fraud grew, and machine-learning tooling made it possible for two Palantir alumni to build a data product with a small team. Market: Brazil Journal's R$9 billion a year of losses is the size of the problem; our estimate of the vendor revenue is that if fraud and false-positive losses are the pool and a vendor can capture 2 to 5% of the losses it removes as fees (our assumption), the revenue pool is about R$180 to R$450 million a year across Latin America; Brazil alone is a share of that. The company's 2022 target of R$3 million of revenue and 50 customers shows the early stage. What was different: Palantir-style data engineering, behavioural features rather than rules, and fees per transaction aligned to the merchant's volume; the competitors were far larger (the sources do not name them; Signifyd, which hired the team, is a leading example). Fit with Norte (our reading): two technical founders with a clear thesis who got Kaszek, GFC and Iporanga around them, and a seed stage where a connector adds investors, which fits the Manifesto's 'follower' role; Norte is named in the 2020 seed (Brazil Journal). Outcome and risks: antifraud is a scale and data game dominated by global vendors, and Legiti's team joined Signifyd in March 2023 within about three years of its seed, with no later activity found, so the venture outcome appears limited; the lesson is that data advantage needs volume that a young company in a niche may not reach before a larger player buys its talent.
note: Read: Brazil Journal 2020-11-30 (16 seconds, R$9bn, two thirds false positives, 'infinite chess' quote, Norte in seed), Canaltech 2022-01-25 (pandemic growth, targets), Signifyd release 2023-03-07 (team move). Arithmetic: 2-5% x R$9bn = R$180-450M; the fee share is our assumption, and applying it to total losses (not to the share a vendor can remove) overstates the pool. Competitor names are not in the sources except Signifyd as the team's new employer. The outcome reading (limited) is our inference from the team joining Signifyd and no later activity. Confidence low.

value: Palomma, based in Medellín, Colombia, says it is building the 'AI-native bank for real estate' in Latin America, starting with rent. It works through real estate agencies in a B2B2C model: AI agents that automate the agency's leasing, sales and collections conversations; a payment gateway specialised in rent that collects from tenants and pays out to landlords and agencies (treasury and disbursement included); Palomma Plus, a rewards programme for tenants; rent guarantees; and Palomma Advance, which gives landlords up to 12 months of rent in advance. Money comes from owning the rent flow and then monetising it with credit, guarantees and insurance (the Y Combinator profile describes this plan; fees are our reading). By November 2026 it served more than 500 agencies and 200,000 tenants, processed about US$130 million of rent a month (about US$1.5 billion a year), and had grown annual recurring revenue from about US$100,000 to about US$3 million in roughly 18 months. The company began as something else. Cipriano Echavarría, a Duke economist from Medellín who sat at David Vélez's old desk at Morgan Stanley, wrote to the Nubank founder, joined Nubank's team in Colombia and learned how to scale consumer banking; with two MIT engineers, Felipe Monsalve (Meta, Bloomberg) and Nicolás Gómez del Campo (J.P. Morgan trading systems), he started a payment method that let people pay online businesses directly from their bank account in Colombia, which was weeks from launch in March 2023 when Y Combinator admitted it to its Winter 2023 batch (US$500,000 from YC, with Latitud and Nido Ventures also backing it). After a pivot, it found its niche in digitising and financing rent (the date is not stated in the Forbes article; a secondary profile says 2024). It closed a US$14 million round in November 2026 led by Cometa (Mexico) with Volpe Capital, Clocktower, Tekton, Simma and Yango Ventures, and returning backers Y Combinator, Nido, Norte Ventures and 17Sigma; US$10 million is recorded as the Series A and the rest as an earlier pre-Series A without date or investors. The funds are to consolidate Colombia, strengthen guarantees and prepare international expansion.

Paraphrased. Figures are the company's. The split of the US$14 million is from earlier notes.

value: The problem: renting is the largest recurring financial flow in Latin American real estate, yet it is run by agencies on manual processes, bank transfers and thin technology, and banks have not designed anything for it. In Colombia, 41% of households live in rented homes (DANE, via Forbes Colombia), the highest share in the region and fourth in the world, which means about 8 million households paying rent and an annual flow above US$30 billion. Landlords wait for payment and want cash early, tenants have little access to credit, and agencies lose time on collections. The logic: whoever owns the rent flow sees the best data on both sides and can sell credit, guarantees, advances and insurance on top, which is why Palomma starts with the agency's software and AI (to win the customer) and with payments (to own the flow), then monetises through financial products. Why now: language models can run the agencies' leasing and collections conversations, bank-to-bank rails (and Pix-like systems) make collection cheap, and the Colombian rental guarantee market is only partly served. Market: the company's figures, relayed by Forbes Colombia, put real estate financial flows in Latin America at US$565 billion a year with rent the biggest and most recurring at about US$205 billion (the YC profile says US$235 billion; the two differ). Our estimate of the revenue pool: its present US$3 million of ARR on about US$1.5 billion of annual rent processed implies a take of only about 0.2%; if financial products raise the blended yield to 0.5% to 1.5% of the rent flow (our assumption), then capturing 5 to 10% of Colombia's roughly US$30 billion would be about US$7 million to US$45 million a year, and 5 to 10% of the region's US$205 billion would be about US$50 million to US$300 million a year. What is different: a focus on one vertical where it owns agencies, payments and credit, a team with Nubank and big-bank experience, and the sector pioneers backing it; competitors named by the source are traditional banking groups such as Grupo Aval and Grupo Bolívar, and rent-guarantee players like CredAluga in Brazil are comparables abroad (from our other research). Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who showed they could pivot, a regional thesis that matches other Norte-backed rental-guarantee companies and a connector role at the early stage; Forbes lists Norte among returning investors, so it backed an earlier round, but no source describes that round. Risks: ARR is small against the US$130 million monthly flow, so margins on payments are thin; credit and advances can bring losses; Colombia is one market and cross-border rent rules vary; and the company has already pivoted once.
note: Read: Forbes Colombia 2026-11-11 (US$565B and US$205B LatAm flows, DANE 41%, 8M households, >US$30B Colombia, competitors Aval and Bolívar, ARR and flow), Y Combinator profile (US$235Bn of rental flows; plan for credit and insurance). Arithmetic: US$3M / (US$130M x 12 = US$1.56B) = 0.19%; 0.5-1.5% x 5-10% x US$30B = US$7.5-45M; x US$205B = US$51-307M. Yield and share are our assumptions; the market figures are the company's relayed by the press, not independent. Confidence medium: market figure from a read source (but company-relayed), differentiation from read pages. CredAluga mention is from our own research for the portfolio, not a Palomma source.

value: A personal assistant service on WhatsApp where human assistants, helped by AI, pay bills, book appointments, buy tickets and run daily errands for affluent Brazilian families on a monthly subscription.

Tempo sells a personal assistant on WhatsApp to Brazilian families who have no time for the "work after work": paying bills and domestic staff, taxes such as IPVA and IPTU, medical appointments and reimbursements, flights, errands and shopping. The customer writes in WhatsApp; a human assistant employed full time by Tempo does the task, helped by AI that handles a first level of the conversation, suggests answers from each client's context and history, and lets one assistant serve more people (the founder says from 5 to 7 clients per assistant in the traditional model to more than 20 with Tempo, with a goal of 3 to 4 times that). Payments run from a prepaid account that the customer tops up and that the assistant uses to pay; every payment needs the owner's approval on WhatsApp, and the account structure is contracted from Celcoin. Tempo makes money from a monthly subscription. When operations began in June 2024 the price was R$490; by April 2025 the entry plan was R$790 a month for one person and R$1,190 for a family, with an average ticket near R$1,100 (Brazil Journal in February 2025 reported about R$1,000, ranging from R$700 to R$2,500). The target is the high-income segments of the banks, such as Itau Personnalite and Santander Unique, and families spending R$30,000 to R$40,000 a month. The idea came from the experience of co-founder and CEO Eduardo Latache, who as a partner at the venture fund Base Partners hired a personal assistant and called it one of his best decisions; he left the fund in early 2024 to turn that experience into a company with Raul Lima, a former CTO of the banking-as-a-service company Bankly. Tempo worked in stealth mode and launched publicly in February 2025 with about 100 paying clients; by April 2025 it had 150 clients, monthly revenue near R$165,000, growth of 40% in the last month, almost entirely by word of mouth, and a team of a little over 30 people (12 in technology and product, about 20 in service). Beyond direct sales, Tempo sees a B2B channel: it already served a family office that offers the service to its clients, four companies were testing it as an employee benefit in February 2025, and companies can hire it for executives. The founder wants to scale with a human in the loop and turn the service into more product and less manual work, possibly with cheaper packages of fewer services. It targeted 1,000 paying clients by the end of 2025 (about R$1 million a month at the then-current ticket). It is backed by Maya Capital, Norte, Caravela Capital and angels, and cites the American company Duckbill as inspiration.
