value: The problem: affluent Brazilian families and professionals carry a daily load of low-value but unavoidable tasks (bills, taxes, domestic payroll, bookings, reimbursements, errands) that a personal assistant solves well, but a human assistant has historically been affordable only to executives. Latache lived this at Base Partners and says the assistant became his most important service provider. The logic: WhatsApp is the main channel of Brazilians and Pix makes small payments instant, so a conversation can be the whole interface, and the prepaid account lets the assistant pay while the owner approves each payment. Generative AI is what changes the economics: if software drafts answers and handles routine steps, one assistant can serve 20 or more people instead of 5 to 7, and the price can fall from a luxury ticket toward the premium-bank customer. The founder compares the idea to Duckbill, a US company that raised a US$25M Series A in 2023 (Startups.com.br), so the model has a foreign comparable, with the difference that in Brazil Pix and WhatsApp replace the credit card. Market size (our estimate): Brazil Journal quotes the founder saying the Personnalite-type segment alone is more than 2 million people. Assumption: if Tempo reached 1% of that segment (20,000 clients) at an average ticket of R$1,100 a month, revenue would be about R$264 million a year (roughly US$47 million at about R$5.6 per US$); at 5% it would be about five times that. The corporate-benefit and family-office channels could widen it, but these are our assumptions and not company figures. A strong outcome is the leader of a new category, with annual revenue in the low hundreds of millions of reais. What is different: unlike a bank concierge or a chatbot, Tempo owns the whole task (human assistant plus AI plus payment account), so it has the context of the client's transactions that, in the founder's words, the bank often lacks; he frames it as 'principality' in the transactional life, not the financial life. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): two experienced founders, one a venture investor who knows the buyers and one a fintech CTO; an early stage where Norte's Manifesto says it helps by connecting people and bringing top funds and angels onto the cap table, which matches the round, where Maya led, Caravela joined and angels such as founders of Trybe, Mottu and UME came in. Risks: the unit economics depend on AI really raising the clients per assistant while keeping the service personal; the price is still high for a mass market; the service depends on WhatsApp's rules and on a third-party payment partner; and the category is young (the same article says another WhatsApp assistant, Alfredo, announced a strategic pause in 2025). Evidence is thin: only two press articles and a Maya Capital post could be read, and the company's own pages could not.

value: GatekeeperX sells software that lets banks, fintechs, payment processors and online merchants decide in real time whether a transaction or a new customer is legitimate, and manage fraud and anti-money-laundering (AML) work on the same platform. Its pitch is to stop the criminals and let the good customers through without friction: a decision engine answers in about 100 milliseconds, using each client's own history compared with millions of similar transactions. The platform brings together four solutions that can be bought separately or integrated: transaction evaluation, monitoring, onboarding and device checks, and disputes. Customers build rules in a visual workflow, test them in simulations before deploying, feed them with native machine-learning models and smart lists that update themselves, and see approval, fraud and anomaly metrics in dashboards with alerts. It also maps fraud rings by linking users, devices and transactions, and uses AI agents that investigate alerts, explain decisions and suggest rule changes around the clock. On 2026-11-11 it launched an MCP connector so that analysts can ask ChatGPT, Claude or Copilot about their real fraud data, simulate rules and manage controls in plain language. The company makes money by selling this software to financial and e-commerce companies, with service levels written into contracts (it cites more than 99.998% of decisions within the expected time). It came from four people, two Argentines and two Colombians, who joined Rappi in the same month about eight years before and built payments and fraud tools there and at Mercado Libre, Stori, Aplazo, Oracle, Idemia and PayU. Carlos Ayalde, who was VP of Payments and Fraud Prevention at Rappi and general manager at Stori, is CEO; the other three leaders on the company page, Renny Hernandez, Martin Moreyra and Diego Nieto, are two engineers and a product leader. They started the company in 2025, and describe it as AI-native from the first day: the team uses AI to prototype and ship and builds agents into the product. Traction: the company announced its arrival in Colombia in January 2026 saying it already processed more than 20 million transactions in more than five countries; by July 2026 it said about 50 million transactions a month; a case on its site says a tier-1 regional acquirer replaced both an external provider and an in-house rules system, gaining 3 points of approval rate and cutting 3-D Secure use by 20% without more chargebacks (company figures). It was named among Forbes Colombia's 100 startups to watch in 2025 and in the Colombia Early Stage 100, has 28 people on LinkedIn, sponsored the Febraban fraud and anti-money-laundering congresses in Sao Paulo in November 2026 as it expands into Brazil, and plans to enter the United States in 2027. Its investors are Monashees, H Twenty Capital, Norte Ventures and, since May 2026, Global Paytech Ventures.

value: The problem: banks, fintechs and online merchants in Latin America lose large sums to fraud and, at the same time, reject legitimate customers. The company cites more than US$80 billion of yearly regional fraud and financial-crime losses and says over 40% of legitimate transactions are rejected for no good reason (company figures, not independently checked). Fraud and AML teams also work in separate tools, so the same account is investigated twice, at different times. The logic and why now: real-time payments (Pix in Brazil, Bre-B in Colombia) leave no time for a manual review, so decisions must be automatic and cheap; and modern AI lets a vendor propose rules, explain decisions and investigate alerts, which the founders say replaces static rule lists run by large analyst teams. The team built exactly these systems at Rappi, Mercado Libre and Stori, so they know what a buyer needs. Market size: a published estimate from an analyst firm, Fortune Business Insights (quoted by Impactotic), puts the global fraud-detection market at US$67.1 billion in 2026 growing to US$243.7 billion in 2034. For Latin America we have no published figure; our bottom-up assumption is 500 to 1,500 financial institutions, processors and large merchants that could buy a platform at about US$100,000 to US$250,000 a year, which gives roughly US$50 million to US$375 million a year. A strong outcome would be a regional leader holding 10 to 20% of that, plus entry into the US. All of these inputs are our assumptions. What is different: one platform for fraud and AML and for identity, device and transaction signals; simulation before deployment; AI agents and an MCP connector for analysts; and local, hands-on service and real-time data delivery. The CEO says it already competes with vendors that have been in the market for ten years, and a published case says it replaced both an outside provider and an in-house system at a regional acquirer. These are company claims. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): operator-founders with deep domain experience, the kind of 'obsessed founders who know more than we do' that Norte's Manifesto says it backs; and a Brazil expansion where Norte's network of operators can open doors to banks and fintechs. Monashees, H Twenty Capital and later Global Paytech Ventures (a payments-focused fund) are co-investors. Risks: long enterprise sales cycles and trust requirements for a vendor that is two years old; incumbents with large installed bases; concentration in a few big customers; and expansion across several countries and regulators with a team of about 28 people.

value: Nomo began in 2021 as a 100% digital mobile operator for Brazilians, an MVNO (a virtual operator that buys network capacity wholesale and resells it) with a native app, no 0800 line and no queues, plans that could be changed, paused or cancelled at any time, and charges only for what was used. Its infrastructure came from Telecall, which represents Vivo, and its first systems were outsourced; the founders wanted to rebuild the software stack of a telecom company the way fintechs like Nubank and Stone had rebuilt banking and payments. The idea came from Henrique Garrido, who had been at Endeavor, NeoAssist and Stone, and from three long-time colleagues from Stone (Gabriel Lima on product, Marcos Augusto on technology and data, and Pedro Geneze on marketing and growth); he decided in April 2020 to start a company and spent a year looking for backers. In November 2021 Nomo closed a round of about R$14 million led by Iporanga Ventures with Norte Ventures and individual investors such as Elie Horn, Ronaldo Iabrudi, the family office of Jacques Nasser and Guilherme Weege, and started operating with 500 test customers and a waiting list of thousands, first in Sao Paulo and Rio. By February 2023 it had several thousand customers with an NPS near 80, a base growing 30% a month and 35% of sales coming from member-get-member referrals. The consumer business was hard to make profitable, mainly because independent MVNOs have no large sales counter behind them and pay a high cost to win customers, so the founders pivoted to selling their technology to other operators. That B2B business, Wave Tech, offers carriers redesigned apps and plans, digital number portability, billing and CRM systems, and software that connects broadband operators to independent fibre networks. In January 2024 it had about R$3 million of annualised revenue from three customers. In January 2024 the listed telecom-software company Bemobi bought 51% of Wave Tech for R$11.5 million (R$4 million new capital and R$7.5 million paid to Nomo, mostly returning the 2021 investors' money), with put and call options on the remaining 49% exercisable in 2029; the three remaining founders stayed on. Mobile Time reported in April 2025 that Wave, run by Garrido as CEO, had contracts with four operators in Brazil, two in Mexico, one in Colombia and one in Chile, that revenue grew 4.5 times in 2024 with the first profit, that it doubled in the first quarter of 2025, and that about 30% of revenue came from outside Brazil. The consumer MVNO, meanwhile, is now run by the Brazilian group Algar through its innovation hub Brain: it had 5,000 customers in May 2025 and about 9,000 lines in December 2025 in five cities, sells mostly through Meta and TikTok and through an AI seller called Nina, and Algar plans to turn the platform into a service for ISPs and other brands.

value: The problem: Brazilian mobile telecom is concentrated (98% of 246 million lines were with three operators in 2021) and customers are unhappy: about 130 million lines change operator every year, according to the partner of Iporanga Ventures quoted by Startupi, and the founders said churn was close to 50%. Legacy systems were built to sell expensive voice minutes to few people and are now used to sell cheap data to many. The logic: bring the fintech playbook to telecom, with a native app, self-service and its own software, and use the MVNO model to sell without building towers. Why now: 5G, regulatory openings and a wave of fintech-trained operators. The team (ex-Stone) had taken a company from zero to IPO, which investors cited as decisive. Market size (our estimate, since no independent figure was read): the consumer route is a share of about 246 million lines but, as the Algar executive says in Mobile Time (2025-12), 'in Brazil the MVNO goes sideways, nobody got it right yet'. The B2B route is smaller but sturdier: Bemobi alone serves more than 100 mobile operators in 50 countries and 200 broadband operators (Brazil Journal 2024). Assuming 300 operators that could pay US$100,000 to US$300,000 a year for apps, billing and portability software, the market is about US$30 million to US$90 million a year, and a strong outcome for Wave is a few percent to 10% of that plus platform services. These are our assumptions. What was different: a product-led team that rebuilt systems and the app experience, an NPS around 80 against a telecom average that the CEO put at about 5% in Brazil, and referral-led growth; later, a vendor that avoids lock-in and multi-year contracts, in the CEO's words 'vendor 2.0'. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): founders with Stone's operating experience, in a concentrated market where Norte could join a round led by a specialist fund (Iporanga) and supply other investors, which fits the Manifesto's idea of putting funds and angels on the cap table at an early stage. Risks, which materialised: consumer MVNOs depend on expensive customer acquisition and thin margins, and the 2021 investors only recovered their money in the 2024 sale (Brazil Journal); the B2B business relies on a handful of operators and on Bemobi's option rights.

value: Kanastra builds the technology and back office for Brazil's private credit market. Companies that lend (fintechs, factoring firms, banks) and the investors that fund them use Kanastra to set up and run structured funds, above all FIDCs (receivables funds), and securitisation products such as CRIs, CRAs, LCAs and LCIs. Before Kanastra, creating a FIDC meant hiring several providers, each doing one part of the process; Kanastra puts fund management, administration and custody, securitisation (issuing, managing and safekeeping the products) and banking services for funds, such as payment accounts, Pix, boletos, CCBs and commercial notes, on one proprietary platform with end-to-end automation and data tools for originators, investors and managers. It earns a commission that Brazil Journal estimates at 0.1% to 0.5% a year on the assets it serves, which at R$35 billion in October 2025 implies roughly R$35 million to R$175 million a year; the company does not disclose revenue. The company was founded in January 2022 by Gustavo Mapeli, who had worked at BNP Paribas in London, BCG and SoftBank, and Manuel Netto, who came from ZX Ventures (AB InBev's innovation arm). The two had already started Kardinal in 2020, a wealth and alternative-assets manager for clients outside the Rio-Sao Paulo axis, and created Kanastra because they originated many structured products and found the back office poorly served. In June 2023, with a US$13 million seed round, it had 35 clients, including Creditas, SolFacil and Patria, and R$2 billion under custody. In 2023 revenue grew 11 times and assets 13 times, to about R$7 billion. In May 2024 it made its first acquisition, Limine DTVM, a fund administration and custody firm, giving the group about 120 vehicles, 100 originators and 300 institutional investors. A R$110 million Series A in June 2024 led by Kaszek was followed in January 2025 by an investment from Itau Unibanco, through Kinea Ventures, together with a commercial partnership in which Intrag DTVM offers fiduciary administration of FIDCs with Kanastra; assets under service then went from R$15 billion to R$35 billion in 2025. In October 2025 a R$170 million Series B led by F-Prime (Fidelity's venture arm), with IFC, financed new products, more automation of liability-side processes such as capital calls, and more clients. At that point Kanastra served nearly 200 clients, including Itau, XP, Banco BV, ABC Brasil, Patria and JGP, with more than 250 operations, and was growing its team by only 35% while assets more than doubled. It has offices in Sao Paulo and Uberlandia, a LinkedIn page with 224 people in November 2026, and its posts show events and product themes such as multi-originator FIDCs and the electronic duplicata, whose testing period runs to January 2027.

value: The problem: Brazilian private credit has grown fast (a 230% rise in five years, according to F-Prime's partner in the Series B announcement) but its operations still run on fragmented providers, manual processes and legacy systems. Each lender that wants to fund itself through a FIDC or securitisation needs an administrator, a custodian, a bank, an escrow account and data reporting, usually from different firms. The logic: the founders originated structured products themselves and saw that the back office, not the origination, was the bottleneck. A single software-led platform with regulatory licences (DTVM, securitiser, banking-as-a-service) can automate the asset side (policy checks already run automatically) and the liability side, and so serve more funds per employee. Why now: private credit is taking share from bank lending, regulators are moving to electronic duplicatas and standardised structures, and fintechs depend on FIDCs for funding. Market size: Brazil Journal (2023 and 2024) estimates the assets under custody and administration of structured funds and securitised products at about R$1.6 trillion, with the largest providers being BRL Trust (R$400 billion, mostly private equity funds) and Oliveira Trust (R$120 billion). At the 0.1% to 0.5% fee range reported there, the fee pool is roughly R$1.6 billion to R$8 billion a year; at R$35 billion Kanastra holds about 2% of the base. If it reached 10% of today's base, revenue would be about R$160 million to R$800 million a year, before market growth. These figures are the press's estimates and our arithmetic, not company disclosures. What is different: it combines fund services, securitisation and banking in one platform, grows with a small team (assets doubled while headcount rose 35%), and is the technology partner of Itau, XP and BV. Competitors named by Brazil Journal are Oliveira Trust, BRL Trust and Vortx in fund administration and custody, and Opea and Virgo in securitisation. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): operator-founders with deep market knowledge, and a seed round in which Norte joined US and Brazilian specialist funds (Valor Capital and Quona co-led) at the stage the Manifesto describes as bringing 'top funds and angels onto cap tables'; Norte's network of fintech operators can help with the originators who are Kanastra's clients. Risks: regulation and licences (Kanastra is a regulated entity, and the rules for FIDCs and duplicatas are changing); competition from larger incumbents and banks building in-house; credit-cycle exposure through its originator clients; and the challenge the CEO names himself, keeping quality as assets grow from R$7 billion to R$100 billion.

value: Dolado began in 2020 as a platform to help small shopkeepers in peripheral neighbourhoods and small towns of Brazil go digital and restock. The idea came from Khalil Yassine, an engineer who left Citi's investment banking in November 2019: on weekends he helped his father's small shop in the north of Sao Paulo and saw him leave the store twice a week to buy goods in the centre of the city, paying cash in a informal market with no bargaining power. With Guilherme Freire and Marcelo Loureiro, who had been studying an Indian inventory start-up and were introduced by an iFood co-founder, he planned a marketplace connecting suppliers to small merchants. The pandemic closed the shops in March 2020, so the first product became a free digital catalogue: the founders went door to door teaching merchants to photograph products and share them, the first client was Yassine's father, and the product spread when a merchant posted it in a Facebook group; it reached 5,000 merchants in six months and had more than 3,000 registered companies and 77% monthly growth when the seed round was announced in December 2020. It made money from a network of partners whose services the merchants used, and used local community leaders, trained as business analysts, to guide shopkeepers. In March 2021 it launched the product that became its core, automatic restocking: instead of only a marketplace, Dolado bought goods from suppliers, mainly mobile-phone and computer accessories from Sao Paulo's popular shopping streets, bundled the orders of many merchants and delivered them through third parties, earning the difference in price. By April 2022 more than 20,000 merchants used it, revenue had grown 19 times in a year and the team had grown from 20 to 100 people in 2021, when it raised a R$53 million Series A led by Valor Capital Group. NeoFeed reported in December 2024 that after the B2B marketplace market turned and large players became indebted, Dolado chose to hold on to cash, a decision it presented as the reason it kept going; the same piece describes it as a platform that connects digital sellers to industry. Today its LinkedIn page describes an ecosystem that accelerates the growth of brands and sellers on marketplaces, with sales-acceleration programmes, a management platform integrated with the sales channels in Brazil and logistics solutions; it has 68 people on LinkedIn, and in October 2026 it organised, with Agent.Shop, the first Agentic Commerce Summit in Brazil in Rio de Janeiro (about 400 registered for 150 seats), a sign of its focus on AI agents that buy and sell. The dates of the change from small shopkeepers to marketplace sellers, the business model today and the current traction figures could not be found in readable sources; the company site does not render without JavaScript.

The founder lived it in his father's shop. The logic: collect many small orders, buy them together from suppliers and deliver, so the merchant saves time and gets better prices and the supplier reaches places it could not; start with a free catalogue to build trust and data, then sell the restocking. Why then: the pandemic pushed small merchants to digitise, WhatsApp was already their sales channel, and venture money was available. Market size (our estimate; no published figure was read): the company had more than 20,000 registered merchants in April 2022 (Startups.com.br). Assumption: if it reached 100,000 merchants and each bought R$5,000 a month through the platform at a gross margin of about 6%, gross profit would be about R$30 million a month, or R$360 million a year. These inputs are our assumptions and the real margin is unknown. What was different: field work with community analysts, a free first product, and an operation that bought and delivered goods instead of only listing them. Comparable companies abroad, as the founders cited, include an Indian inventory start-up for small shops. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): a founder from a merchant family with an investment-banking background, supported by Valor Capital, Global Founders Capital and angels from iFood, Stone and Olist, in an early round where Norte's connection to founders and angels from those companies is the kind of value the Manifesto describes. value: Brazilian credit-infrastructure company that lets retailers and other businesses offer their own consumer credit under their own brand, covering funding, risk models, Pix payments and AI-run collections.

Ume is a Brazilian credit-infrastructure company that lets retailers, marketplaces and service businesses offer their own credit to their customers, under their own brand, and keep the financial profit that normally goes to banks and card issuers. The platform covers the whole credit cycle: the legal and funding structure of each operation (including access to capital-markets funding through FIDC funds), credit policy and risk modelling, a sales and payment layer integrated with Pix, and customer service and collections run largely by AI agents. The site says the proprietary neural-network credit model has run since 2017, that about 95% of customer service is automated, and that the company handles over 270 thousand tickets a month. The company began inside academia: its first idea was a PhD thesis at UFMG, by computer scientists including Marco Cristo, on using a deep neural network to price credit better for one of the largest retailers in northern Brazil. Berthier Ribeiro, a former partner at Méliuz and ex special-situations analyst at BTG, heard about it through his father, the computer scientist Berthier Ribeiro-Neto, and set out to take it to market. From 2019 Ume operated in Manaus as a lender, taking the risk itself: a digital 'crediário' (store instalment credit) for regional retailers with revenue of R$40 million to R$500 million a year, where the consumer downloaded the app, was approved in about five minutes and could split a purchase into up to four instalments, and the retailer was paid in two days for a discount fee, while Ume also earned interest from the consumer. In 2021 it lent R$26 million to 47 thousand people; in 2023 it lent R$220 million through more than 2,000 retailers. Its edge in this period was a lower default rate (30% under the crediário average, its CEO said in 2024) and, from 2024, payment by Pix QR code, which cut transaction costs compared with private-label card competitors such as DMCard. After a seed round in April 2022 it expanded from the North to the Northeast, then to the South and Centre-West, and in 2025 it changed its model from being a lender itself to being the infrastructure that lets other businesses run their own credit. By September 2025 it had about 6,000 partner stores and expected R$1 billion of annualised volume that year. In 2026 its site reports more than 4 million users, over 10 thousand points of sale, R$1.2 billion of credit granted in 2026 and over R$850 million raised from investors in equity and debt, and the company expects R$2 billion of volume in 2026. Backers include NFX, Canary, BigBets, Clocktower Ventures, Norte Ventures, PayPal Ventures, Globo Ventures, FJ Labs, Valor Capital Group and Bewater; loans are funded by FIDCs bought by institutions such as Itaú, Bradesco, XP, Credit Saison, Western Asset, Verde and Milenio. Berthier Ribeiro-Neto joined as CTO in 2024. The Series B was meant to fund proprietary technology, AI infrastructure and commercial scale, and to expand beyond retail and, later, to other countries.

value: Problem: in Brazil, store credit ('crediário') is a large market, estimated by Ume's co-founder at about R$200 billion a year in 2022, but it was run by a few large retailers; most mid-sized and regional retailers sell on card instalments, so the issuer keeps the credit margin and the retailer carries the cost of the sale. Ume's CEO says 80% of the 300 largest retailers do not offer credit at the point of sale. Logic: a retailer already owns the customer, the sale and the data, so it is the natural originator of credit if it can get what it lacks: a credit model, funding, collections and a payment rail. Ume sells all of that as one service, so it can earn from the credit spread and platform fees without the retailer building a financial arm. Why now: Pix is cheap and instant, FIDCs let institutional money fund consumer receivables, and AI makes customer service and collections far cheaper per account. Market size and share (our estimate): the R$200 billion figure comes from the company's own co-founder (Brazil Journal 2022), so treat it as an upper bound. Ume expects about R$2 billion of volume in 2026, roughly 1% of that figure. If the infrastructure model reaches 5% of a R$200 billion market, that is R$10 billion of annual volume; at an assumed 4 to 8% net revenue on volume (our assumption, from credit spread plus fees), that would be R$400 to 800 million of yearly revenue. These are assumptions, not company guidance. What is different: the team started as a lender, so it has six years of default data and a neural-network credit model built by PhDs (the CEO claims 30% fewer defaults than the crediário average and 30% more approvals at the same risk), and it has already raised R$850 million-plus from equity and debt investors, including large Brazilian institutions. Competitors named: DMCard (private-label cards, the segment leader in 2024), BaaS and credit-as-a-service providers (some are partners, per the CEO), and banks. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it invests in obsessed founders and in networks, and brings top funds onto cap tables. Ume's seed in 2022 was co-led by US funds (NFX, Canary) with Norte participating, and later rounds brought PayPal Ventures, Valor and Bewater, the kind of syndicate a connector-style seed investor helps assemble. Risks: credit losses in a downturn or a higher-rate cycle, dependence on FIDC funding appetite, regulation of credit and of Pix instalments, and big banks or card networks entering the same niche. The business also burned cash while growing, so the shift from lender to infrastructure must prove its unit economics.

Brazilian fintech whose platform lets investment advisers and family offices create tailor-made investment products from fractions of fixed-income and credit assets, using tokenisation and AI.

Nexa is a São Paulo fintech that builds tailor-made investment products for the clients of financial advisers, family offices and wealth managers. Instead of picking from a shelf of standard products (CDB, COE, LCI, CRA, funds), an adviser describes what a client wants to achieve, such as a monthly income from 2028 or cash for a child's studies abroad in 2027, and Nexa assembles a product from fractions of existing assets chosen for risk, term, liquidity and cash flow. The assets come from institutional originators and include credit-card receivables, trade receivables (duplicatas), consortium quotas, payroll-type loans and loans backed by the FGTS severance fund; the company says it rejects 90% to 98% of the opportunities it reviews. Assets are securitised and tokenised on a blockchain, which lets it split them into very small pieces (down to R$1) and regroup them to match each client. The CEO calls the result a 'mini-ETF'. The company holds licences for asset management, securitisation and distribution, buys assets through an FIDC fund and carries them until they are resold. It earns a margin on each product, which the CEO compares to an investment bank's, with the take rate varying by operation. The founders are Lucas Danicek (CEO, formerly at Nest and Pátria, then at Tera, the family office of Pátria's founders), Eduardo Furuie (fixed income and credit at Pátria and Tera) and Bernardo Mascarenhas (a former M&A and debt-capital-markets banker who founded the credit start-up Noverde, later bought by Dotz, and stayed at Dotz until 2024). The company was set up in early 2024 and ran in beta until mid-2025, when it began to look for its first clients: multi and single family offices and offices of independent advisers. By July 2025 it had three institutional clients and expected to move R$500 million in 2025 and R$1 billion in 2026. In February 2025 it launched tokens that replicate exclusive funds of single family offices and wealth managers. In October 2026 it launched Nexa Genesis, a platform in which an AI turns a plain-language request into a product in about two minutes, so advisers can create products without waiting for Nexa to structure them. The company said it had issued 375 products by the end of August 2026 and 800 by the end of September, that it had grown about 25% a month for two years, and it projects five-fold growth in 2027. Its site says partners hold more than R$200 billion in assets under management. Backers are Norte Ventures (since the pre-seed), MAYA Capital (which led the R$25 million seed in July 2025), Newtopia, Clocktower Ventures, Kiara Capital and Citrino Ventures, and in 2026 Valor Capital Group and Citrino made a further investment of undisclosed size. A new round is planned for 2027. The offer today is fixed income and private credit in reais and dollars, with shares and other assets to be added.

value: Problem: advisers and family offices in Brazil serve clients with different goals, tax situations and cash-flow needs, but the products they can distribute are standard shelf items made for a mass audience, so each client has to fit the product. Large investors get tailor-made structures from banks; smaller wealthy clients do not. Logic: if assets can be securitised, tokenised and cut into small fractions, a platform can combine them into a product built around one client's goal at low cost, and software (now AI) can do the structuring that used to take a team. Why now: the regulatory and technical base for securitisation and tokenisation in Brazil is maturing, the number of investment advisers has grown from 4,565 in 2016 to about 27,000 and independent offices need ways to stand out, and generative AI lets the structuring be done in minutes. Market size and share (our estimate): the company says its partners hold more than R$200 billion under management (its site). ANCORD counted 26,679 credentialed advisers in September 2026, of whom about 6,300 are not tied to institutions (26,679 minus 20,413). The CEO's own arithmetic (Brazil Journal 2025) is 100 adviser offices with R$2.5 billion each, a 5% share of wallet and a 5% take rate, giving R$500 million of yearly revenue, which that article's reporter calls aggressive. A more careful version: R$250 billion of assets at 100 offices, 5% share = R$12.5 billion a year placed, at a 1% to 2% take rate (our assumption, close to the 1% scenario Brazil Journal used) = R$125 to 250 million of revenue. A strong outcome is therefore a business with revenue in the low hundreds of millions of reais, not a mass-market one, unless it moves into distribution to end clients. What is different: it builds the product from the client's goal and sells to advisers, not to end investors; it controls originating, curating and securitising (licences for management, securitisation and distribution), and its founders come from Pátria and Tera, so they know the buyers and originators. Competitors and comparables: other tokenisation and fixed-income distribution platforms in Brazil, bank-run structured products and the large brokerages' shelves. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders and works as a connector, bringing top funds onto cap tables and helping to generate revenue from day zero. Norte was in the pre-seed and followed in the seed, led by MAYA, which fits that follower-and-connector pattern; an experienced founding team with access to originators and family offices is where the network matters. Risks: the model needs funding, distribution and intellectual capital at once, and an industry executive told Brazil Journal that it risks adverse selection if other channels reject its products; take rates are thin and scalability is doubted; tokenisation rules are still evolving; and its volume figures are the company's own and unaudited.

Brazilian company that offers employers a single platform for flexible employee benefits, HR management and corporate expenses, with a card and app that let workers choose how to spend their benefits budget.

Flash is a São Paulo company that sells companies one platform for employee benefits, people management and corporate expenses. It began as the 'flexible benefits' alternative to the meal and food vouchers of Alelo, Sodexo (now Pluxee), VR and Ticket (Edenred): the employer sets a monthly budget and the worker spends it where they choose, on one pink Mastercard-branded card and an app, instead of several single-purpose cards. Today the product is three connected lines: benefits management (multi-benefit card, transport vouchers, PAT-compliant meal and food benefits, health and well-being partners, a discount club), HR management (admission and dismissal, recruiting with AI, time and attendance) and expense management (corporate card, reimbursements, expense reports). The company says its card has zero fee, and it earns from the benefits and card business and, increasingly, from software subscriptions for HR and finance. The idea came to Pedro Lane while he tried to give meal vouchers to the staff of his own agency and saw that workers accepted losing part of the value (receiving R$400 for each R$500 voucher) to turn the benefit into cash, in a market where a few incumbents held about 95% of it and had little reason to innovate. He built the company with his brother Guilherme Lane, who handled technology, and Ricardo Salem, who became CEO. Work began at the end of 2018 and the product launched in July 2019 with clients from the start, aimed first at small and mid-sized companies that the large incumbents neglected. Seed money came in January 2019 from Kevin Efrusy, Patrick Sigrist and Guilherme Bonifácio (iFood's founders) and Global Founders Capital, and a Series A followed at the end of 2019 led by Monashees; in total the company had received about US$9 million in its first year. In July 2020 it served 60 thousand people at 1,500 companies; the pandemic brought new services such as mental-health support, bill payment and home-office purchases. By mid-2021, after 700 days, it had about 200 thousand users at about 4,000 companies and expected to move R$2 billion that year. A US$22 million Series B led by Tiger Global (June 2021) turned it into an all-in-one HR platform, and a Series C of more than US$100 million led by Battery Ventures and Whale Rock (March 2022) paid for product and hiring; the team then had 300 people. It bought ExpenseOn (July 2022) to enter expense management and FolhaCerta (March 2023) to build its time-tracking module. In August 2024 it had over 30 thousand client companies and 1 million users, and by May 2026 about 60 thousand companies and 1,300 employees, half of them in revenue-generating roles, after growing its operation more than 15 times since the Series C. The company says it has generated cash for almost a year, announced a R$400 million investment plan, and in August 2026 raised a R$150 million Series D led by Battery Ventures and Kevin Efrusy with Endeavor Catalyst joining. Its goal is to lead the benefits market by 2030; it counts on new PAT rules, which cap the fees charged to merchants and shorten payment terms and are meant to open the market to challengers, and plans to use AI to integrate HR and finance tasks and to resume acquisitions. Mexican business-data platform that gives lenders and fintechs API access, with customer consent, to small businesses' tax, financial and company data, for credit-risk analysis, factoring and KYB/KYC.

Syntage is a business-data platform that lets banks, fintechs and software companies in Latin America connect, with the company's consent, to the public and private data of their small and mid-sized business customers, through APIs and a dashboard. Its core is Mexican: it logs into the SAT (the tax authority) to pull a company's electronic invoices (CFDI), tax returns and compliance status, validates credentials in about three seconds and extracts invoice data in minutes, then adds other public and private sources and builds indicators on top. The site presents three main uses: credit-risk analysis (a personalised report of indicators, with updates and alerts when risk indicators change), factoring (verifying invoices, with notices of cancellations, credit notes and payments, and monitoring financed invoices) and KYB, KYC and anti-money-laundering checks (original documents, blacklists, and links between businesses and their shareholders). It sells to lenders, so its revenue comes from institutional customers integrating the API; the site says more than 400 financial institutions use it and that it holds the ISO 27001:2022 security certificate. The company began in early 2020 as Satws (SAT Web Services), a product focused only on Mexico and SAT data, founded by Matheus Pedroso, a former CTO of the Mexican fintech Credijusto, and Sebastian Carlsson, who had led LenddoEFL in Latin America after a career in corporate investment banking. Pedroso built the technology and Carlsson sold it, based on what they had seen at both companies about gathering business information to onboard customers and assess risk. By mid-2021 a team of five served about 60 institutional customers, with no churn, and was close to break-even. A seed round of US$4.3 million, co-led by Nazca and Costanoa Ventures with QED, RaliCap, Latitud and ten angels, was announced in August 2022, together with the rebrand to Syntage and a plan to add private and public sources and other Latin American countries from the fourth quarter of 2022. Satws then had about 150 institutional customers. Costanoa describes the platform as covering open finance and credit intelligence across Latin America, and a Costanoa-listed client, the corporate-card company Clara, reports faster card approvals (about 24 hours on average) after moving to Syntage from other data providers that could not extract all CFDIs and connected slowly. A directory profile says the company has analysed more than 250,000 businesses; this figure and the count of customers vary between pages (300+ on a directory page, 400+ on the company site).

value: Problem: Mexican lenders and fintechs that serve small businesses lack reliable financial records for them: many firms are informal or keep thin books, bank statements are partial, and manual document collection slows onboarding and invites fraud. Mexico has one rich, standardised source of truth, the SAT's electronic invoices, which show a firm's real sales, customers and payments, and which firms can authorise a lender to read. Logic: a lender that can read a firm's invoices in minutes can underwrite faster, verify factoring invoices, and monitor risk over time; the same data supports KYB and anti-money-laundering checks. Selling this as an API means each lender does not build and maintain its own SAT connection, which is slow and breaks when the SAT changes. Why now: open-finance and fintech lending have grown in Mexico, factoring and working-capital lenders need invoice data, and a data layer can be extended to other Latin American tax and company registries. Market size and share (our estimate): INEGI's 2024 census counted about 7 million establishments in Mexico; in the private sector there were 5.47 million economic units in 2023, and 64.3% of them were informal, which leaves roughly 1.95 million formal units (5.47 million x 35.7%, our arithmetic). Those are the businesses whose data a lender could pull. On the customer side, Syntage says more than 400 financial institutions use it. If those pay an average of US$20 to 60 thousand a year (our assumption, typical for API data products sold to lenders, not a reported figure), that implies about US$8 to 24 million of annual revenue today; reaching 1,500 institutions across Mexico and a few Latin American markets at similar prices would give US$30 to 90 million. This is the realistic scale of a data-infrastructure business of this kind unless it expands into broader data products or per-query pricing for a much larger number of businesses. What is different: it started narrowly (only SAT data, only Mexico) and went deep, with a fast and complete SAT connection that a client such as Clara preferred over other providers, then widened into a platform with indicators and KYB features; it holds a recognised security certification, important for lenders; and it was backed by specialist early-stage funds (Nazca, Costanoa, QED, Latitud). Competitors and comparables: other Mexican open-finance and tax-data connectors exist (they were not described in the sources we read, so we do not rank them), and large credit bureaus and KYC vendors could add similar features. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does and connects them with funds and people; a two-founder team with credit and technology experience building infrastructure for Latin American lenders fits a follower role beside US and Mexican early-stage leads, but we found no source describing Norte's role. Risks: dependence on one government interface (a change in the SAT's rules or access policy could break the core product), concentration in Mexican fintech lending, which can cool, regulatory limits on data sharing, and the small size of the seed financing relative to the scope of the vision.

Brazilian cybersecurity company with a self-service platform that scans a company's domains, websites, servers and cloud accounts, finds weaknesses and guides their fix, without installing agents.

Unxpose is a São Paulo cybersecurity company that sells a self-service platform to find and fix security weaknesses, aimed especially at companies without a large security team. It needs no agent installation: a customer creates an account, connects its assets (domains, websites, servers, cloud accounts) in minutes, and the platform scans them continuously, lists what is exposed, explains how to fix it, and produces a one-click report that shows its security posture to customers or auditors. It integrates with tools such as Slack, Teams, Jira and Splunk so vulnerabilities can be handled in a company's existing workflow. The product has grown into a set of modules sold as one platform: Attack Surface Management (finding all subdomains, websites, hosts and services of a company that are visible on the internet and their weaknesses), Cloud Security Posture Management (checking cloud accounts against industry frameworks and privacy rules), SaaS Security Posture Management (checking that employee accounts follow good practice and whether company credentials leaked in breaches), Security Questionnaires (AI that proposes answers from past questionnaires, to cut the time spent on customer security reviews) and Third Party Risk Management (sending and tracking questionnaires to suppliers). Pricing in 2021 started at R$2,500 a month, by subscription. The site says hundreds of companies of all sizes around the world use it, and a customer case from CAF (a development bank) praises its visibility and low cost and the ability to check cloud changes in staging. The company was started by Josemando Sobral (CEO), Tiago Assumpção and Patrick Costa. It received a first investment from Canary in March 2021 and used it to develop its new product and grow sales. In September 2021, during a wave of ransomware attacks on Brazilian companies (Lojas Renner, Fleury, JBS), it launched 'Você Protegido', a free online test that gives a company an exposure score from its domain, covering web, DNS and leaked credentials, as a taster of the full product. In October 2025 it was one of 11 start-ups chosen from Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Mexico for the first Google for Startups Accelerator: AI for Cybersecurity in Latin America, an equity-free programme. Public sources give no revenue, customer count or further funding; directory sites list small amounts of total funding (about US$320 to 360 thousand), which we did not rely on.

Logic: attack-surface and posture scanning can be automated and sold as subscription software that a non-expert connects in minutes, so it can be priced for the mid-market and sold to many customers with little services work. Why now: cloud and SaaS adoption multiplied the number of places data can leak, regulation of data protection (LGPD) and customers' vendor-risk demands push companies to prove their security, and AI helps with questionnaire answers and fix guidance. A strong Brazilian outcome of 3% to 5% of that segment would be R$25 to 100 million of annual revenue; reaching North American mid-market customers (which the company's English site targets) would enlarge this, but we found no evidence of its sales there. Brazilian infrastructure company for Open Finance and Pix: it runs the regulatory side of Open Finance for banks and fintechs and lets them initiate Pix payments, including the new Pix modes (biometrics, tap to pay, recurring), earning a fee per successful transaction.

Iniciador is a São Paulo payments-infrastructure company that sits between Brazilian banks, fintechs and platforms and the Central Bank's Open Finance and Pix rails. It holds two Central Bank licences, payment institution and payment initiator (ITP), and its customers use either its licences or their own on top of its technology. The platform has two sides. On the regulatory side it runs, as a managed service, what an institution must operate to take part in Open Finance Brasil (authorization server, consent management, monitoring, certifications, directory registration, ticket handling). On the product side it lets customers initiate Pix payments from the payer's own bank (the 'Pay by Bank' flow) and receive bank data, with newer Pix modes built on top: Pix por Biometria and Pix por Aproximação (tap to pay), Pix Automático (recurring payments such as subscriptions) and Smart Transfers (account sweeping by rule or balance). Revenue is tied to success: a fixed amount, some cents, for each successful transaction on a customer's platform. The company was founded in 2021 by Marcelo Martins, a serial entrepreneur who had already founded and sold a start-up, and Guilherme Decampo, who leads technology; the registry shows the company opened in December 2021. A first round of R$1.2 million, made soon after founding by industry specialists and angels (Edson Santos, former head of Global Payments in Brazil, and Andres Bilbao, co-founder of Rappi), financed the start. The company is a founding member of Open Finance Brasil and sits on its board representing ABFintechs. As the Central Bank released new Pix modes (Pix Inteligente in April 2024, Pix por Biometria in February 2025, Pix Automático in June 2025) Iniciador followed each, and in August 2025 it said it served about 60% of the payment initiators taking part in Pix Automático and more than half of those authorised for Pix por Biometria, with customers including iFood, Stone, Nomad, Núclea, Magie and Jota, and a customer base four times larger than in early 2025. Its 2026 site says one in three Pix initiations in Brazil run on its infrastructure and about 1.4 billion data requests a month, and lists customers such as PagSeguro, CloudWalk and Wise (these figures are the company's own). In August 2025 it raised R$32 million led by Valor Capital, with big_bets, Alter Global, Actyus and Norte Ventures, to invest in technology and scale, to hire, to add the capital the Central Bank requires of licensed institutions and to start targeting large banks. In May 2026 it launched what it calls Brazil's first agentic-payments MCP on Pix, which lets an AI agent propose a payment that the user approves by biometrics, together with an AI toolkit and an embedded-engineers service.

value: Problem: since the Central Bank opened Open Finance and then Pix by initiation, every bank and fintech that wants to offer 'Pay by Bank', Pix por Biometria or Pix Automático must connect to dozens of institutions' APIs, pass certifications, keep monitoring regulatory metrics and maintain it all every time the rules change. Few have the engineers or the licence to do so, and a failed redirect or consent costs them the sale. Logic: Iniciador sells that burden as a service and earns a few cents on each successful transaction, so its revenue grows with the volume that flows through its customers. Why now: Pix initiation volume jumped from R$3.2 billion in 2024 to R$15.3 billion in 2025 (Banco Central data reported by Finsiders), and the Central Bank keeps adding modes (Pix Automático in 2025, instalment Pix expected next), each of which needs a new integration that Iniciador can ship once for all customers. Market and reachable share: Pix moved R$26.9 trillion in 63.8 billion transactions in 2024 (Febraban and Abecs, quoted by Startupi). Our own estimate: if initiation-based Pix reaches 5% to 10% of that count (3 to 6 billion transactions a year, our assumption) and the infrastructure layer earns R$0.10 to R$0.30 per transaction (our assumption; the company only says 'some cents'), the Brazilian fee pool is about R$0.3 to R$1.9 billion a year (roughly US$55 to US$340 million at the 2025 average rate of 5.59). A player that keeps its claimed one-third of initiations would reach about R$0.1 to R$0.6 billion, or US$19 to US$114 million: a business worth backing but not a giant on its own, with upside from data, regulatory services, agentic payments and other Latin American open-finance systems. Different: in the sources it is the only player that sells both the regulatory operation and the payment products, it has Central Bank licences, it holds a founding-member seat and a board seat at Open Finance Brasil, and it reports approval rates above 95% (company figures). Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): founders who know the regulatory plumbing better than an investor does, a B2B network business in which introductions to banks, acquirers and funds matter, and a round led by a top fund (Valor Capital) with Norte as one of several funds, in line with Norte's wish to bring the best funds onto cap tables. Risks: dependence on one regulator's rules (a rule change or a bank-built alternative can shrink the layer), customers who internalise the integration once volume is large, thin per-transaction fees, and capital requirements for a licensed payment institution. The sources name no competitor, so differentiation rests on company claims.

value: Brazilian beverage group that holds niche brands (Praya beer, Mamba canned water, Baer-Mate mate soft drinks), now backed by Heineken's production and distribution through Heineken SPIN.

Better Drinks is a São Paulo beverage group that builds a portfolio of niche brands meant not to compete head-on with the big incumbents (Ambev, Coca-Cola) but to ride trends such as sustainability, convenience and lower sugar. It was launched on 1 February 2022 by two former Ambev executives, Felipe Della Negra (CEO, earlier head of Red Bull in Brazil and of Kraft Heinz in Italy) and Felipe Szpigel (Chief Growth Officer, who had left Ambev in 2018 to start the ready-to-drink brand F!VE), by merging five independent brands whose founders became shareholders: Baer-Mate (a mate-based soft drink without added sugar), F!VE (ready-to-drink cocktails), Mamba (canned water), Praya (premium wheat beer created in Rio in 2016 by four surfer friends) and Vivant (canned wine). Together the brands had sold more than R$50 million in 2021, the group started with R$25 million from the founders and angels (among them the Zee.Dog founders, the head of Domino's Pizza in Brazil, executives of Cia. Tradicional de Comércio and Norte Ventures) and set out to reach R$1 billion in revenue by 2026. The group sold through supermarkets, bars and restaurants and online (about a third each in early 2023, in 30,000 points of sale), and added brands such as Vermelhão, an aperitif launched in April 2022 with the singer Gusttavo Lima that became half of its revenue in 2023. It raised about R$65 million in sustainability-linked private debt from W Capital in March 2023, tied to CO2-reduction targets, and estimated an addressable market of R$52 billion. In June 2024 Heineken Brazil became a minority shareholder, without a cash injection, offering its production, purchasing and distribution structure and a path to a larger stake as each brand hit sales and sustainability targets; the group became the 'impact brands' pillar of Heineken SPIN, and its site shows its B Corp certification. Heineken began brewing Praya in 2025 and producing Mamba Water in January 2026, and Mamba's yearly revenue grew from R$10 million in 2024 to about R$100 million in 2026 (NeoFeed). F!VE and Vivant have had no sales since 2024 and are expected to be discontinued. In November 2026 NeoFeed reported that Heineken signed to buy control for R$500 million in cash, all ordinary shares held by 67 shareholders, with Della Negra keeping a non-voting stake, subject to approval by the competition authority Cade, and with plans to take Praya abroad.

value: Problem: Brazil's beverage market is dominated by a few giants that control shelf space, distribution and bars, while small brands with good ideas (a lighter beer, a canned water, a mate soft drink) lack the scale, logistics and purchasing power to grow beyond a niche. Logic: Better Drinks pools such brands under experienced beverage operators, so that they share overheads, buying and sales teams, and pursue consumer trends the incumbents are slow to serve, then hands growth to a partner with a distribution network. Why now: the 2022 start came when younger consumers were moving to lower-alcohol, canned, sustainable and ready-to-drink products and when marketplaces and delivery apps made it easier to reach buyers without the big distributors. Market and share: the company estimated in 2023 an addressable market of R$52 billion, about a third of all beverages in Brazil, growing about 15% a year (Brazil Journal, CEO's figures; not independently checked). Our own check: that is the company's claim, and no independent report was read, so we treat it as an upper bound. Reachable share: the founders' target of R$1 billion in sales by 2026 would be about 2% of R$52 billion; the evidence is that the group reached about R$48 million annualised in 2022 and that Mamba alone reached about R$100 million in 2026, which suggests several hundred million reais is reachable, not R$1 billion for the group as built. The outcome that did arrive, Heineken buying control for R$500 million in cash (about US$90 million at the 2025 rate of 5.59), is a far smaller outcome than the R$1 billion in revenue the group once planned (we do not know Norte's return, since its stake is not disclosed). What is different: a team that had run Red Bull, Ambev and Kraft Heinz operations, brands with strong identity (Mamba is compared by the press to the US canned-water brand Liquid Death, a comparable valued at about US$700 million, according to Startups.com.br), a B Corp certification and sustainability-linked debt, and the structure with Heineken that supplied production and distribution. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): experienced operators who know the industry better than an investor, an angel-style cap table around a network (Zee.Dog's founders, restaurant and retail executives), and Norte as one of many names rather than the lead, in line with its 'size of the pie, not the piece' approach. This is also a consumer company in a portfolio otherwise built on software and fintech. Risks: capital-intensive, low-margin physical distribution; heavy concentration in one brand (Vermelhão was half of revenue in 2023, a product tied to a celebrity); dependence on the big players for shelf and production; and brands that stalled (F!VE, Vivant), with the cash needed to rescue them. Confidence is low because market size is a company claim and the competitors come from one article.

value: E-commerce logistics company that runs urban warehouses and its own software to store, pack and deliver online brands' orders in Mexico and Brazil, with pick-up points, B2B distribution and cross-border import services.

Cubbo is an e-commerce logistics company that stores, packs and delivers online orders for brands, and sells the software it built to run that work. It started in Mexico City in January 2021, founded by two Colombians, Brian York (CEO) and Josu Gurtubay (COO), who saw that large foreign direct-to-consumer brands wanted to ship to Latin American shoppers without opening local operations. The idea was to fit out urban warehouses close to customers, so that a brand integrates its store (Shopify, VTEX, Mercado Libre and others), sends stock to Cubbo and has each order picked, packed and delivered, including same-day, cross-docking and returns. Over time it added a B2B operation for brands that supply retail chains, an importer and merchant-of-record service for brands that want to sell in a new country without a local entity, a network of pick-up points called Cubbitos, and software it builds in-house (WMS, OMS and TMS), part of which it licenses white-label to carriers in Colombia and Chile. Revenue comes from storage, handling and delivery fees plus software. Cubbo reached Colombia in November 2021 with a US$4 million seed round led by SV LatAm Capital. In March 2022 it bought DedaLog, a profitable São Paulo fulfillment start-up whose CEO, Tiago Pavan, became its country manager in Brazil, and in mid-2022 it closed an undisclosed pre-Series A round with SV LatAm Capital, Gerdau Next Ventures, Gaingels and Community Access Fund, saying it had raised US$8 million before it (the seed is US$4 million, so some other funding, perhaps a bridge, is unreported) and that revenue had grown 274% since the seed. In Brazil it now runs five warehouses (Embu das Artes, Itapeva, Cachoeirinha, Manaus and Extrema, the last two opened in 2026), serves more than 120 customers there (the company names Natura/Avon and L'Oréal among its customers) and says its Brazilian business grew 310% from 2024 to 2025. Across Mexico and Brazil it reports about 300 brands, more than a million orders a month and a projected global revenue of about US$68 million for 2026 (company figures reported by Startups.com.br). In Mexico it opened an 8,850 m² centre in Tultepec in August 2026 (investment of MX$18 million, capacity of 450,000 orders a month) and in September 2026 started a pilot with OXXO to use its convenience stores as Cubbitos pick-up and return points, on top of more than 3,500 active points. Newer products include Cubbo Engage, an AI tool for support, sales and post-purchase, and an MCP for customers to connect their own AI models. The company says it plans more warehouses in Brazil (Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo, Recife and the Centre-West) and a bigger role in B2B.

value: Problem: online brands in Mexico and Brazil, especially small and mid-sized ones and foreign brands entering Latin America, struggle with logistics. They need local stock for fast delivery, handling at peak events such as Hot Sale and Black Friday, returns, and customs and tax rules, and few can build warehouses and software in each country. Marketplaces solve it but take commissions and the customer relationship. Logic: Cubbo takes the physical work (urban warehouses near shoppers) and the systems (WMS, OMS, TMS, integrations with stores and carriers) and charges per order and storage, so its revenue grows with each brand's sales while cost per order falls with density. Why now: online sales keep growing in both countries and brands want to sell on their own channels as well as marketplaces; Cubbo adds pick-up points (OXXO) and B2B flows that link the same inventory to retailers. Market and share: Mexican retail e-commerce reached MX$941 billion in 2025, up 19.2% (AMVO's Estudio de Venta Online 2026), and Brazilian e-commerce R$235.5 billion in 2025, up 15.3%, with 438.9 million orders (ABIACOM). Our own estimate of the outsourced-fulfillment pool: logistics (storage, handling and last mile) is roughly 10% to 15% of order value and 20% to 40% of it is outsourced to a third party (both our assumptions). Mexico: 941 x 10-15% x 20-40% = MX$19 to MX$56 billion, about US$1.0 to US$3.1 billion at roughly 18 pesos per dollar (our assumption). Brazil: 235.5 x 10-15% x 20-40% = R$4.7 to R$14.1 billion, or US$0.8 to US$2.5 billion at 5.59 (2025 average). Together about US$1.8 to US$5.6 billion; the projected US$68 million of 2026 revenue (company figure) would be 1% to 4% of it, so a leader's share of a few more points is plausible, but the figure is a coarse estimate. What is different: it operates in two of the region's largest markets with its own software and its own warehouses (the Brazilian network is described as run mostly by people, with software for efficiency instead of robots), has customers such as Natura/Avon and L'Oréal, and is building extra layers (Cubbitos, merchant of record, Engage). A competitor named in the press is Melonn (Mexico and Colombia), focused on small businesses; Amazon's logistics and marketplace fulfilment are the obvious alternatives. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): operator founders who know the problem better than the investor, a business that depends on introductions to brands, retailers and co-investors in several countries, and a cap table of local and regional funds and angels (SV LatAm Capital, BluStone, Gerdau Next Ventures and founders of Latin American start-ups), consistent with Norte's follower and connector role. Risks: logistics is capital-intensive and low margin, with fixed lease and labour costs before volume arrives; customers can concentrate in a few large brands; Amazon, Mercado Libre and large carriers can undercut it; and the 2022 plan to raise a Series A was not matched by a round we could find, so funding of the growth is not visible. Confidence is low because market size is our estimate and company revenue is a projection.

value: Frizata is a frozen-food company from Rosario, Argentina, that makes its own ready meals and ingredients and sells them directly to consumers through its online store, with home delivery, instead of through supermarkets. It calls the model a digitally native vertical brand (DNVB): it controls the whole chain, from factory and product design to online sale and delivery, and uses customer data and reviews to change the range quickly, treating each food as a product that gets new versions, like software. The catalogue is aimed at 'flexitarians', people who eat meat but want more vegetables and less impact: vegetables and fruit, appetisers, pizzas, empanadas and meat-free alternatives, with around 50 products in 2021 and almost 80 by 2022. The site today sells ready meals, packs and discounts in Rosario, Buenos Aires and Córdoba. It was founded in 2019 (Forbes Brasil says 2018) by Adolfo Rouillon (CEO) and José Robledo, friends since university in Rosario and serial entrepreneurs who had already founded and sold other companies (Congelados del Sur and Amtec.net, according to Forbes Argentina). In its first twelve months it reached 30,000 customers, revenue was about US$10 million in 2020 with a US$15 million run rate in mid-2021. In July 2021 it announced a Series A of R$25 million (about US$4.65 million) led by SP Ventures with Marcos Galperin of Mercado Libre, Jaime Soler Bottinelli (former global CEO of Cencosud), Gonzalo Ramírez Martiarena (former global CEO of Louis Dreyfus), Glocal AgriFood Tech and Norte Ventures, to expand abroad. It had entered Chile earlier in 2021, began selling in Greater São Paulo in July 2021 (importing from its Argentine factory) and planned a first online store in San Francisco in September 2021. The international plan then slowed: in 2022 it put Chile and the United States on hold because of freight costs and currency problems, and in October 2023 it said it would focus on São Paulo for three to five years, with revenue of about R$100 million (over US$20 million), 90% from Argentina, Chile and the United States and 10% from Brazil, and 70% of products made at its own factory. In June 2026 Descubre.vc reported, from Argentine press, that it had paused its global expansion (Brazil, Chile and the United States) because of higher logistics costs and would concentrate on Argentina, keeping its direct-to-consumer model, serving Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Rosario and investing 900 million pesos to optimise its plant with artificial intelligence.

value: Problem: frozen food is a large category in which supply has hardly changed in years. A long chain of producers, distributors and supermarkets limits which products reach shelves, so new, healthier, vegetable-based or more convenient dishes struggle to get listed, and producers learn little about who buys what. Logic: Frizata sells direct, so it can launch and test products fast, use customer data to improve them, capture the retailer's margin and offer lower prices, and use its own factory to control cost and quality. Why now: the pandemic pushed households to buy food online and to keep stock at home, and interest in vegetable-based eating was growing; in 2021 the company was already making about US$10 million a year and growing in several cities. Market and share: the only market figure we read is a paid-report summary from IMARC, which puts Brazil's frozen-food market at US$5.9 billion in 2025, growing about 3.2% a year to 2034; we treat it as a rough order of magnitude, since the method is not visible. No comparable Argentine figure was found. Our own estimate for direct-to-consumer: if online brands take 1% to 3% of Brazilian frozen sales (our assumption), the pool is about US$60 to US$180 million a year in Brazil alone; the company's reported Brazilian sales were 10% of about US$20 million, or about US$2 million in 2023 (AgFeed), so the Brazilian opportunity was far from captured, and a strong outcome would be a few tens of millions of dollars of Brazilian revenue plus the Argentine business, not a regional giant. What is different: a factory of its own with direct delivery and a wide range of vegetable-based products, plus founders who had built and sold two companies. A natural comparison is the plant-based and flexitarian food brands abroad, but we found no sourced comparable outcome. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): experienced founders who know the industry better than the investor, a cross-border expansion in which Norte's network in Brazil could help hiring, partners and co-investors, and a Brazilian lead investor (SP Ventures) with Norte as one of several funds, in line with its follower role. Risks, which later events confirm: perishable cold-chain logistics are expensive, imported products from Argentina suffer from freight costs and currency swings, and the company paused the expansion into Brazil, Chile and the United States in 2022 and again in 2026; the 2026 refocus on Argentina means the Brazilian thesis behind the 2021 round has not materialised. Confidence is low because market size comes from a paid-report summary and the company's recent figures are missing.

value: Brazilian maker of open-source financial infrastructure: Midaz, a ledger for core banking, plus modules for onboarding, risk, reporting and reconciliation, sold to fintechs and financial institutions, earning from hosting, features and services.

Lerian is a São Paulo company that builds modular financial infrastructure for fintechs, payment institutions, credit operations and banks, with an open-source core at its centre. Its first product, Midaz, is a ledger, the database where a financial institution records, reconciles and audits every transaction, and the heart of a core banking system. Because the code is open, a customer can audit and customise it and avoids vendor lock-in, and Lerian charges not for the software itself but for hosting it, for added functions, and for implementation, support and consulting. Around the ledger it has added tools for onboarding and compliance orchestration (Flowker), real-time transaction risk (Tracer), regulatory reporting (Reporter) and transaction reconciliation (Matcher). Its site now groups the offer as core banking (accounts, balances, fees, Pix, boleto, TED, bill payment, regulatory reports), credit (product design to payment, with automatic accounting), multi-source reconciliation, and its own messaging connections to the Central Bank, Nuclea, Dataprev and the courts, plus professional services to design, migrate and run the architecture; it also offers a path for companies leaving banking-as-a-service to operate under their own licence. It was started by Fred Amaral, a co-founder of the payments company Dock, with two former Dock colleagues, Jefferson Rodrigues (CTO) and José Zapata (named as co-founder in 2024 coverage; the 2026 coverage lists Maísa Amaral, HR director, as the third partner). Coverage disagrees on the start (2023 in Startups.com.br and Finsiders; January 2024 in Brazil Journal and Baguete); the company began as a product-technology consultancy, which in eight months served six clients and found they all lacked control over their transactional database, which led to Midaz. Midaz was launched in July 2024 as, in the company's words, the first open-source ledger for core banking in the world, and the company says it offers 32 modules that can be contracted separately. In November 2024 it raised R$18 million, one of the largest seed rounds of the year in Brazil, led by MAYA Capital with Quartz, Supera Capital, Norte Ventures, Crivo Ventures and angels, enough for about two and a half years, to hire engineers. In January 2026 it raised a further R$30 million (US$5.5 million per Finsiders) in an oversubscribed seed, again led by MAYA with Norte Ventures, Supera Capital, Crivo Ventures, BluStone and Kevin Efrusy, a partner at Accel, to apply AI to the platform, build sales and customer success and start positioning abroad. Within 24 to 36 months the company plans to enter other Latin American markets and the United States.

value: Problem: small and mid-sized banks, payment institutions and fintechs in Brazil depend on third-party core banking platforms, which are closed, are priced per account and per transaction (a poor fit when the regulator or competition stops them charging customers for Pix, for example), and offer little flexibility, while the largest players (Nubank, Inter and the incumbents) build their cores in house. Many fintechs also outgrow banking-as-a-service and must take their own licence and operate their own connections to the Central Bank. Logic: Lerian offers a modular, open-source ledger plus the connections and tools around it, and earns on hosting, features and services, so the customer controls the code and Lerian's revenue grows with the platform's use instead of with a licence fee. Why now: more fintechs are moving from banking-as-a-service to their own licence, the Central Bank keeps adding rules and rails that need maintenance, and cloud-native, AI-assisted development lowers the cost of building such software. Market and share: one market-research summary (Market Research Future, which sells the report) puts Brazil's core banking solutions market at US$640 million in 2025 and US$2.17 billion by 2035, a 13% yearly growth; other editions of the same report and other research firms give very different numbers, so we treat it as a rough order of magnitude and not as fact. A comparable outcome abroad: Visa agreed in 2023 to buy Pismo, a Brazilian cloud-native core banking and issuer-processing platform, for US$1 billion in cash (Visa press release), which shows that a strategic buyer values the category. Our own estimate: if Lerian reached 5% to 15% of the Brazilian market by 2035 (our assumption), that is US$110 to US$325 million a year of revenue at that report's figure; Latin American and US expansion would add to it. What is different: a team with experience in Dock's infrastructure and in the design of Brazil's instant-payment systems (its site says its founding team helped design the architecture of Latin America's largest payments platform and Brazil's instant payments), an open-source model that reverses the usual pricing, and its own messaging layer for Central Bank connections. Named competitors are Pismo (Visa), which Lerian says it wants to beat, and the established core banking vendors in the report above. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): serial founders with deep domain knowledge, who know the problem better than an investor; a network business in which introductions to banks, fintechs and funds count; a Norte partner quoted by Startups.com.br says Lerian is 'exactly the type of start-up we look for: serial entrepreneurs, passionate about solving acute pains' and that Brazil has a clear 'right to win' in global financial infrastructure, and Norte joined both rounds led by MAYA, which fits its role of one of several funds on the cap table. Risks: long and trust-heavy sales cycles to regulated institutions; competing with Pismo, which now has Visa's distribution; an open-source model that makes it easy to copy or to use without paying (the licence terms were not checked); and a small team with a product line growing quickly. Confidence is low because the company is two years old, with no published revenue or customer count, and market size comes from a vendor-sold report.
